column6: Erik Paul "LASE" Perez, Toofly, Duro, Kekoa, Lorena Barrezueta, Ramon Trevino
column13: Back in 2007, the schoolyard of PS/MS 34 on Manhattan's Lower East Side was just grey concrete until a grant from the youth center Generation Xcel launched the very first "Dream Walls" project. Street artist Erik Paul "LASE" Perez gathered a crew including Kekoa, Toofly, Duro, Lorena Barrezueta, and Ramon Trevino to turn the walls into a canvas of possibility. At that time, the neighborhood was still shaking off its gritty past and becoming more family focused, and the school wanted to inspire its K-8 students with public art. When the sun filters through the yard, its rays still catch the bold, imaginative lines Kekoa painted. His vibrant work became a daily source of wonder for the children streaming in from the surrounding blocks, and that personal connection between artist and community is why the mural still feels alive today.

column6: Erik Paul "LASE" Perez, Toofly, Duro, Kekoa, Lorena Barrezueta, Ramon Trevino
column13: You might not guess it, but this second piece by Kekoa was painted during that same 2007 Dream Walls initiative, which helped launch Thrive Collective's citywide mural movement. The Lower East Side had long been a hub for graffiti and street art, but PS/MS 34 was one of the first public schools to embrace it as a teaching tool. Standing before this mural, you feel the enduring power of that community dream. As a Thrive Collective Creative Director, Kekoa's art helped transform the schoolyard, and in the years that followed, PS/MS 34 earned an A rating from the city. You are seeing more than paint on a wall. You are seeing the seed of a movement that would spread across New York, all because a few artists believed a splash of color could change a child's world.

column6: Erik Paul "LASE" Perez, Toofly, Duro, Kekoa, Lorena Barrezueta, Ramon Trevino
column13: When artist Lorena Barrezueta Carlo first painted in this schoolyard back in 2007, the Lower East Side was a place of reinvention, from tenement immigrant waves to punk rock to today's vibrant mix of old and new. Her mural "Opportunity" gained new meaning when she returned to PS/MS 34 in 2025 to create an updated version. Lorena poured hope into every brushstroke, and this became the 700th mural in Thrive Collective's incredible journey. Returning nearly two decades after her first visit, Lorena captured the spirit of a community that refused to give up. Inspired by the classic Disney style of Mary Blair, her mural includes the Teddy Roosevelt quote "Do what you can, with what you have, where you are." That quiet, powerful message is for every student walking through the gates of PS/MS 34.

column6: Erik Paul "LASE" Perez, Toofly, Duro, Kekoa, Lorena Barrezueta, Ramon Trevino
column13: Picture the Lower East Side in 2007. The neighborhood had been the birthplace of hip hop graffiti in the 1970s, and by then it was negotiating between its rebellious roots and new development. Into that scene stepped Toofly, a pioneering Ecuadorian American female graffiti artist at a time when very few women were recognized in New York's male dominated street art world. Her mural "Xpress" at PS/MS 34 is a defiant, beautiful act of self expression. Known as a "Love Warrior," she poured her signature style into this wall. It was here, on this very spot, that she first helped a generation of Lower East Side students learn to see themselves as artists. Decades later, she still returns to the school, her work a colorful shout out to the graffiti legends who started it all and a warm invitation for kids to find their own voice.

Visit the original Welcome mural blog to experience the entire project from start to finish, including the initial student submissions, design drawings, and a weekly photo journal throughout the process.

On October 28, 2012, Hurricane Sandy ravaged PS 329, causing $1 million in damages and four months displacement. One year later, 350 students, parents, and volunteers from five community partners painted an 825 square foot schoolyard mural, co-designed by 250 students and celebrating Coney Island’s extraordinary resilience after the storm. Watch the story behind the mural here. On this page, enjoy community reflections and the final portfolio of the project.

Think about your own school or home for a moment. What do you see, hear, taste, smell, and touch? That is exactly the question Principal Magalie Alexis asked her students at PS/MS 282 in Park Slope back in 2014. The historical context here is important. At that time, schools across Brooklyn were looking for ways to celebrate student identity and build stronger communities. Over several months, 700 students submitted drawings, photos, family sayings, poems, and stories about their cultures, traditions, and favorite foods. Art director Sam Wisneski took hundreds of those responses and wove them into a single design. Then 400 parents, teachers, and volunteers showed up with paintbrushes over ten weeks to bring "Community: I Am 282" to life on the schoolyard wall. Sponsors like the Coach Foundation and Citi Group helped make it happen, but the real magic came from the students seeing their own words and images reflected back at them. When you stand before this mural, you are looking at the beating heart of a school that truly believes every child belongs.

McKinley Jr. High School in Bay Ridge has seen generations of Brooklyn families walk through its doors, and the "Generations" mural was created in 2014 to honor that long history. Art director Sam Wisneski led the project at a time when Bay Ridge was changing but still holding tight to its strong immigrant roots and tight knit community feel. The mural process brought together current students, alumni, parents, and local seniors to share what the neighborhood meant to them across different eras. One student might have drawn their grandmother's first apartment, while another painted the corner deli where everyone says hello. The result is a colorful conversation between past and present, painted right on the schoolyard wall. When you look at "Generations," you are not just seeing art. You are seeing a bridge between the Bay Ridge of yesterday and the Bay Ridge of tomorrow, built by the hands of the people who live there.

Here is a simple truth. Every child deserves to see themselves reflected in the world around them. That belief drove the "Identity: I Am Mount Eden" mural at PS 170 in the West Concourse neighborhood of the Bronx in 2014. The historical context is significant. The Bronx had long been stereotyped in the media as a place of struggle, but the families of Mount Eden knew their community was full of love, culture, and resilience. Under the direction of artist Sam Wisneski, students answered questions about who they were and what made their neighborhood special. They drew their families, their favorite bodegas, the sound of Spanish music from open windows, the smell of home cooking. Those personal stories became the mural's design. Over ten weeks, students, parents, and volunteers turned grey brick into a celebration of Mount Eden identity. When you stand before "I Am Mount Eden," you hear the students loud and clear. They are saying we are here, we are proud, and this is our home.

Picture Williamsburg, Brooklyn, in the 1940s. Thousands of Puerto Rican families were arriving, bringing bomba music, Spanish language, and a deep cultural pride that would reshape the neighborhood for generations. Fast forward to 2014, and students in the "Mural: Master Class" at Progress High School decided to honor that legacy. Under the guidance of artist Sam Wisneski and art teachers Damon Wiggins and Daisy Schiff, thirty students created a mural at the entrance of the Borinquen Plaza Senior Center, a gathering place for Puerto Rican elders. The project was funded by City Council Member Erik Martin Dilan. The historical connection runs deep. The students painted images that celebrated the pioneers who came decades earlier, and something beautiful happened along the way. Several students told their teacher they wanted to start volunteering at the senior center. They got to know the elders whose history they were painting. When you look at "Williamsburg's Legacy," you are seeing a conversation across time, young hands honoring old stories, and a community refusing to forget where it came from.

column1: Coney Art Walls: Under the Sea
column13: The boards of the Coney Island boardwalk have heard a century of footsteps, from carnival barkers to families eating soft serve. In 2015, they welcomed a different kind of visitor. Street art legend Chris Daze Ellis, a pioneer of the 1980s graffiti scene, came to Coney Art Walls to create "Under the Sea" with help from local students. The historical context is deep. Coney Island had just undergone a revival, and the Coney Art Walls project was turning the neighborhood into an outdoor museum. Daze, whose real name is Chris Ellis, rose to fame alongside Basquiat and Keith Haring, but here he was on Stillwell Avenue, spray can in hand, teaching a new generation. Students watched as he transformed a wall into a dreamy underwater world, full of waves and sea creatures painted in his signature soft, dreamlike style. When you look at this mural, you are seeing a passing of the torch. A legend sharing his gift with the kids of Brooklyn, right there where the ocean meets the amusement parks.

column2: Bronx Studio School for Writers and Artists
column13: Sometimes a word can become a promise. In 2015, the Bronx Studio School for Writers and Artists in Hunts Point invited artists Domingo Zapata and Sam Wisneski to create a mural simply called "Thrive." The historical context here is essential. Hunts Point had long been known for its wholesale markets and industrial landscape, but it was also a community of hardworking families raising children who deserved beauty and inspiration. Zapata, a Spanish born painter known for his vibrant, expressionist style, partnered with Wisneski to lead students through the design process. They asked the young artists what thriving looked like to them. Some drew gardens growing between buildings. Others painted families laughing together. The finished mural on the exterior wall became a daily reminder for every student walking through the doors. No matter what the outside world says about your neighborhood, you can still grow. You can still thrive.

Behind every grand celebration is a quiet act of gratitude. In 2015, artist Kekoa created an interior mural at PS/MS 282 in Park Slope for the school's annual Thrive Gala. The historical context is meaningful. By this time, PS/MS 282 had already become a model for how public art could transform a school community. The gala was a chance to say thank you to the teachers, parents, volunteers, and sponsors who made projects like "Community: I Am 282" possible. Kekoa, who had been part of the original Dream Walls project back in 2007, brought his signature bold lines and playful imagination to this indoor wall. Students watched as their school's hallway turned into a celebration of collaboration. When you stand before this mural, you are seeing a love letter to everyone who shows up. The custodians who unlock the doors, the principal who says yes, the parents who bring cookies, and the kids who pick up a paintbrush.

Walk into the Thomas Jefferson Educational Campus in East New York, and you will find a mural by Kekoa that asks a simple question. What does it mean to thrive? The year was 2015, and East New York was a neighborhood often overlooked by the rest of the city. It had high poverty rates and low media attention, but it also had families who refused to give up. This interior mural was part of Thrive Collective's series of school projects, and Kekoa worked directly with students to design a piece that felt like theirs. They painted images of graduation caps, open books, and hands reaching upward. The historical context is important because East New York was beginning to see new investments in schools and housing, but the community knew that real change had to come from within. That is what this mural says. It says we are here, we are studying hard, and we are going somewhere.

column2: World Academy for Total Community Health High School
column13: The World Academy for Total Community Health High School in East New York has a name that sounds like a promise. In 2015, artist Kekoa helped that promise come alive with an interior mural called "Welcome to W.A.T.C.H." The historical context is specific. W.A.T.C.H. was a small school within the Thomas Jefferson Educational Campus, focused on training students for careers in health and wellness. The mural was painted at a time when East New York was fighting for better healthcare access and more resources for young people. Kekoa led students through a design process that asked them what health meant to them. Some drew family meals. Others painted running tracks and yoga poses. The finished work greets everyone who walks through the school's doors. When you look at this mural, you are seeing a community taking care of itself. A school that says health is not just a class you take. It is a way of life.

Marie Roberts came to Coney Island in 2015 with a paintbrush and a vision. Her mural "Innovators" at the Coney Art Walls project celebrated the thinkers, dreamers, and builders who changed the world. The historical context is electric. Coney Art Walls had turned the neighborhood into a living gallery, with major artists creating works just steps from the Cyclone roller coaster. Roberts, a contemporary artist known for her bold colors and empowering imagery, worked alongside local students to bring "Innovators" to life. They painted portraits of inventors, scientists, and artists, alongside nameless heroes like single mothers and community organizers. When you stand before this mural, you can almost hear the distant screams of the Thunderbolt and the crash of waves on the beach. It is a reminder that innovation is not just for history books. It happens every day in Coney Island, in every classroom and corner store.

column1: IS 117 / TYWLS: I Am Mount Hope
column13: In 2015, two schools shared one building and one powerful idea. IS 117X and the Young Women's Leadership School in Mount Hope, Bronx, came together to create "I Am Mount Hope" with artist Naomi Kuo. The historical context is layered. Mount Hope is a neighborhood that often gets reduced to statistics about poverty or crime, but the people who live there know a different story. They know about block parties, church choirs, and grandmothers who walk kids to school every morning. Kuo, a Taiwanese American artist known for her community based practice, spent weeks listening to students share their stories. They talked about the smells of their grandmothers' cooking, the sound of Spanish and English mixing in the hallways, and the pride of being from the Bronx. The interior mural became a declaration. I am Mount Hope. I am not a statistic. I am a student, a sibling, a friend, a future.

column10: 1210 Parque Mexico Sur, Playas de Tijuana, 22500 Tijuana, B.C., Mexico
column13: Across the border, in Playas de Tijuana, Mexico, a different kind of mural story unfolded in 2015. Artist Sam Wisneski traveled to Escuela Secundaria No. 5 to create "Campeones," which means Champions. The historical context is powerful. Tijuana had long been mischaracterized in American media as dangerous, but the people of Playas knew their city as a place of art, culture, and family. Wisneski worked with Mexican students to paint an exterior mural celebrating their heroes. Not just famous athletes or musicians, but everyday champions. Parents who worked two jobs. Teachers who stayed late. Kids who walked to school every day despite long distances. When you look at this mural, you are seeing art that crosses borders. It says that no matter which side of the fence you live on, every child deserves to feel like a champion.

Butterflies are small, but they can travel thousands of miles. In 2015, artist Sam Wisneski returned to PS 102, The Bay View School in Bay Ridge, to create "Thrive: Bay Ridge," and a butterfly became the mural's quiet symbol. The historical context connects back to 2011, when Wisneski had led the "Welcome" mural at the same school. By 2015, Bay Ridge was changing. New immigrant families were arriving from China, Mexico, and the Middle East, while old school Italian and Irish families stayed put. The question Wisneski asked students was simple. What helps you grow? Answers came in many languages. A butterfly emerging from a cocoon. A seedling pushing through concrete. A hand reaching for a book. The exterior mural became a promise. No matter where you come from, Bay Ridge is a place where you can transform.

The hallway of I.S. 117 Joseph Wade in Mount Hope, Bronx, used to be just a place to pass through. In 2015, it became a destination. Artist Sam Wisneski led Thrive After School art students in creating "Thrive: Mount Hope," an interior mural. The historical context is important because after school programs across New York City were facing budget cuts. But at IS 117, the arts were holding on. Wisneski worked with students who stayed late, ate snacks, and picked up paintbrushes instead of going home to empty apartments. They painted what thriving looked like to them. Some painted family portraits. Others painted college diplomas and career uniforms. One student painted a picture of her mother's hands. When you stand before this mural, you are not just looking at art. You are looking at children choosing creativity over chaos, one brushstroke at a time.

column10: 465 New Dorp Ln, Staten Island, NY 10306
column13: Hurricane Sandy had torn through Staten Island in 2012, and three years later, the scars were still healing. In 2015, artist Sam Wisneski went to New Dorp High School to create "Thrive: New Dorp," an interior mural. The historical context is raw. New Dorp and other Staten Island neighborhoods had been devastated by the storm, with homes destroyed and lives lost. The high school had become a shelter and a gathering place for a community piecing itself back together. Wisneski asked students what survival looked like. They painted waves that did not win. They painted houses with lights on. They painted neighbors helping neighbors. The mural became a quiet monument to resilience. When you look at it, you are seeing kids who lived through something terrible choosing to paint hope instead of fear. That is what thriving looks like on Staten Island.

Every student at PS 721K in Gravesend, Brooklyn, has been asked a version of this question. Where are you going? The school serves students with special needs, and in 2015, artist Sam Wisneski helped them answer with paint. The exterior mural called "Where are you Going?" was a collaborative project that asked students to imagine their futures. The historical context is often overlooked. Students with disabilities are frequently told what they cannot do. They are talked about rather than listened to. Wisneski flipped that script entirely. He asked each student to draw where they wanted to go. Some drew the beach. Some drew a college campus. One student drew a kitchen because they wanted to be a chef. Their answers became the mural. When you stand before this wall, you are seeing children who are used to being defined by their challenges defining themselves by their dreams instead. Where are you going? Everywhere.

Four schools. One lobby. One mural. In 2015, artist Stephen Uhey led 100 students from four different high schools inside the Springfield Gardens Educational Complex in Queens. The Preparatory Academy for Writers, Excelsior Preparatory Academy, George Washington Carver High School for the Sciences, and Queens Preparatory Academy all came together to paint "Thrive: Springfield Gardens." The historical context is unusual. Most murals serve one school community, but this building housed four, each with its own culture and identity. Uhey knew he needed to find what they shared. He asked students what Springfield Gardens meant to them. They talked about the Rochdale Village co op, one of the largest housing cooperatives in the world. They talked about Sunday dinners and summer block parties. They talked about being Black and brown and proud. The interior mural became a meeting place. A reminder that even in a building with four schools, you are one community.

column6: Chris Daze Ellis, Sam Wisneski, Anthony Perez
column13: Coney Art Walls in Coney Island, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2016 called "Cycloptic Merman," created by legendary street artist Chris Daze Ellis along with Sam Wisneski and Anthony Perez. The historical context is about collaboration. This was the second consecutive Coney Art Walls project for Thrive Collective. Daze's concept blended two iconic Coney Island characters, the Cyclops and the Mermaid, into one central figure. He then invited students, interns, and teaching artists to design the surrounding vignettes depicting Coney Island traditions and culture, giving them creative control over their concepts. The resulting collaborative piece at 3050 Stillwell Avenue is a show stopper. When you look at it, you are seeing a legend share his canvas with a new generation. That is how art stays alive.

The McKinley School in Dyker Heights, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2016 called "I Am Brooklyn," created by artist Jessica Olah. The historical context is about local pride. Dyker Heights is known for its holiday lights and tight knit Italian American community, but Brooklyn is so much more. Olah painted the Brooklyn Bridge, brownstones, pizza slices, and the iconic "I Am Brooklyn" phrase. The mural at 7805 7th Avenue is a love letter to the borough. When you look at it, you are hearing a Brooklyn accent. I am Brooklyn. You are too.

PS 236 in Mount Hope, Bronx, got a mural in 2016 called "Welcome to PS 236," created by artists Kekoa and Peach Tao. The historical context is about making a good first impression. The entrance to a school should say "you belong here." The artists painted a bright, colorful welcome sign with smiling faces and open arms. The interior mural at 1871 Walton Avenue is a handshake. When you walk through the doors, you are being greeted. Welcome to PS 236.

PS/MS 183Q in Arverne, Queens, got a mural in 2016 called "I Am the Rockaways," created by artist Marissa Molina. The historical context is about recovery. Hurricane Sandy had devastated the Rockaways in 2012, and four years later, the community was still rebuilding. Molina painted the beach, the boardwalk, and the resilient faces of the people who stayed. The exterior mural at 2-45 Beach 79th Street is a declaration. When you look at it, you are hearing a community say "I am the Rockaways. I am still here."
