PS 58X in Tremont, Bronx, got a mural in 2016 called "I Am East Tremont," created by Pilar Batista and Sam Wisneski. The historical context is about neighborhood identity. East Tremont has been through hard times, but the people are proud. The artists painted local landmarks, families, and the words "I Am East Tremont" in bold letters. The exterior mural at 459 East 176th Street is a passport. When you look at it, you are seeing that this neighborhood is not a problem to be solved. It is a home to be celebrated.

Clemente Soto Velez Cultural Center on the Lower East Side got a mural in 2016 called "Give Thanks," created by artist Sam Wisneski. The historical context is about gratitude. The center is named for a Puerto Rican poet and activist, and it has been a hub for Latinx culture for decades. Wisneski painted hands folded in thanks, surrounded by images of family, food, and community. The interior mural at 107 Suffolk Street is a prayer. When you look at it, you are being reminded to say thank you. For everything.

The National Youth Worker Convention in Cincinnati, Ohio, got a mural in 2016 called "Arise," created by Sam Wisneski with Victoria Cruz and Nico Collazo. The historical context is about the people who serve young people. Youth workers are often invisible, but they change lives every day. The artists painted figures rising from the ground, arms reaching toward the sky. The interior mural at 525 Elm Street is a sunrise. When you look at it, you are seeing the moment when tired youth workers find the energy to go one more day. Arise.

Lutheran Elementary School in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2016 called "Seeds of Love," created by Sam Wisneski and Kaves. The historical context is about faith. The school is church affiliated, and the artists painted a garden where love grows from small seeds into big trees. The interior mural at 440 Ovington Avenue is a parable. When you look at it, you are learning that love is not a feeling. It is something you plant, water, and watch grow.

column10: 655 W 34th St, New York, NY 10001 (Jacob K. Javits Convention Center)
column13: Movement Day Global Cities Conference at the Jacob K. Javits Convention Center in Hell's Kitchen, Manhattan, got a mural in 2016 called "Love and Serve," created by Sam Wisneski and Kekoa. The historical context is about urban leadership. The conference brought together city leaders from around the world. The artists painted hands washing feet, neighbors helping neighbors, and the words "Love and Serve." The interior mural at 655 West 34th Street is a mission statement. When you look at it, you are being asked a question. How will you love and serve your city?

PS/MS 34 in Loisaida, Manhattan, got a mural in 2016 called "I Am Loisaida," created by Sam Wisneski, Leslie Rios, and legendary graffiti artist Crash. The historical context is about the neighborhood's name. Loisaida is the Spanglish pronunciation of Lower East Side, a term coined by Puerto Rican activist Bimbo Rivas. The artists painted the neighborhood's history, from tenements to murals to community gardens. The exterior mural at 730 East 12th Street is a dictionary. When you look at it, you are learning a word. Loisaida. It means home.

MS 42Q in Arverne, Queens, got two murals in 2016. The first was "Arverne, Dream Big," created by Sam Wisneski and Marissa Molina. The historical context is about a small neighborhood within the Rockaways. Arverne is often overlooked, but the students wanted to be seen. The artists painted local streets, the beach, and the faces of students. The interior mural at 488 Beach 66th Street is a megaphone. When you look at it, you are hearing Arverne say "I am here."

column6: Sam Wisneski, Marissa Molina, Sonic, DAZE
column13: The second MS 42Q mural was "Keep Calm Move On," created by Sam Wisneski, Marissa Molina, Sonic, and DAZE. The historical context is about resilience after Hurricane Sandy. The famous "Keep Calm and Carry On" poster was adapted to say "Keep Calm Move On," because in Arverne, you cannot just carry on. You have to move forward. The interior mural at the same address is a mantra. When you look at it, you are being told that the storm is over. Keep calm. Move on.

column6: Sam Wisneski, Pilar Batista, Nico Collazo
column13: Park Slope Tabernacle in Brooklyn got a mural in 2016 called "Fuel," created by Sam Wisneski, Pilar Batista, and Nico Collazo. The historical context is about spiritual energy. The church wanted to remind its congregation that faith is fuel. The artists painted flames, engines, and people running races. The interior mural at 98 5th Avenue is a gas station. When you look at it, you are filling up your tank. Now go.

column6: Sam Wisneski, Ritchie Kong, Nico Collazo
column10: Union Square Park, New York, NY 10003
column13: NYC Well Launch in Union Square Park, Manhattan, got a mural in 2016 called "Holidays Thrive," created by Sam Wisneski, Ritchie Kong, and Nico Collazo. The historical context is about mental health. NYC Well is a mental health hotline, and the launch event was during the holidays, a time when many people struggle. The artists painted bright colors, smiling faces, and the word THRIVE. The exterior mural in Union Square Park is a lifeline. When you look at it, you are being reminded that even in the darkest season, you can thrive.

column2: Bronx Studio School for Writers and Artists
column13: Bronx Studio School for Writers and Artists in Longwood got a mural in 2016 called "Voice of the Bronx," created by Sonic and Sam Wisneski. The historical context is about art and writing. The school focuses on creative expression, so the mural featured quotes from student writers alongside images of artists at work. The interior mural at 928 Simpson Street is an anthology. When you look at it, you are reading the voices of the Bronx. They are loud. They are beautiful. They matter.

PS 104 in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2016 called "Brooklyn Gives," created by Sophia Reed, Kaves, and ADM. The historical context is about generosity. Bay Ridge is a neighborhood of immigrants who came with nothing and built everything. They know the importance of giving back. The artists painted hands giving food, books, and time. The exterior mural at 9115 5th Avenue is a checkbook. When you look at it, you are being asked to write your own check. What will you give?

column10: 888 Rev James A Polite Ave, Bronx, NY 10459
column13: PS 333 and PS 335 in Longwood, Bronx, shared a building and got a mural in 2016 called "I Am Longwood," created by William Acevedo and Sam Wisneski. The historical context is about two schools becoming one community. The artists asked students from both schools to share what Longwood meant to them. They painted bodegas, basketball courts, and grandmothers watching from windows. The interior mural at 888 Rev James A Polite Avenue is a treaty. When you look at it, you are seeing that even when you share a building, you can still be one family. I am Longwood. We are Longwood.

column1: I Am Harlem: Past, Present, Future
column6: Aleathia Brown, Marissa Molina, Nico Collazo
column13: I Am Harlem: Past, Present, Future was created at Harlem Village Academies High School in 2017, with art direction by Harlem's own Aleathia Brown along with Marissa Molina and Nico Collazo. The historical context is about honoring the full arc of Harlem's story. Students explored the concept during after school workshops in the spring, developing design ideas that wove together images from the Harlem Renaissance, the civil rights era, and the vibrant present day community. Community volunteers helped execute their vision in the fall. The mural at 35 West 124th Street is a time machine. When you look at it, you are walking through Harlem's past, living in its present, and building its future all at once.

column10: 133-25 Guy R Brewer Blvd, Jamaica, NY 11434
column13: MS 72Q, the Catherine and Count Basie School in Rochdale, Queens, got a mural in 2017 called "Five Be's," created by artist Jef Star. The historical context is about character education. The school's core values were the five Be's. Be respectful. Be responsible. Be safe. Be caring. Be ready. The artists painted each Be as a colorful pillar, holding up the school community. The mural at 133-25 Guy R Brewer Boulevard is a constitution. When you look at it, you are reading the laws of this school. Live by the five Be's.

column2: High School of Telecommunications, Arts, and Technology
column13: I Am NYC was created at the High School of Telecommunications, Arts, and Technology in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, in 2017 by artist Jessica Olah. The historical context is about the identity of New York City. The students explored what it means to be a New Yorker. Answers ranged from the obvious, subways, pizza, yellow cabs, to the deeper, resilience, diversity, and dreaming big. The mural at 350 67th Street is a love letter to the city. When you look at it, you are hearing the sound of a million voices saying the same thing. I am NYC.

Welcome to Bay Ridge was painted at Fort Hamilton High School in 2017 by artist Jessica Olah. The historical context is about a neighborhood that is often overlooked. Bay Ridge is not a tourist destination, but it is home to generations of families. Olah painted local landmarks like the Verrazzano Bridge, Shore Road, and the 86th Street shops. The mural at 8301 Shore Road is a welcome sign. When you look at it, you are being invited into a neighborhood that is proud, quiet, and strong.

column2: Bronx Studio School for Writers and Artists
column13: Breathe Free, NYC was created at the Bronx Studio School for Writers and Artists in Longwood in 2017 by artist Julia Cocuzza. The historical context is about the stress of city life. New York is loud, fast, and crowded. The students wanted a reminder to breathe. Cocuzza painted deep breaths as colorful waves, with a figure standing calm in the center. The mural at 928 Simpson Street is a meditation app. When you look at it, you are being told to inhale, exhale, and remember that you are free.

PS/MS 42Q in Arverne, Queens, got a mural in 2017 called "Love Well," created by artist Marissa Molina. The historical context is about the quality of love. It is not enough to love. You have to love well. The students explored what loving well looks like. Listening, forgiving, showing up, and being kind. The mural at 488 Beach 66th Street is a relationship manual. When you look at it, you are learning that love is a verb. Do it well.

Rising Stars by the Sea was painted at Dr. Richard R. Green in Arverne, Queens, in 2017 by artist Marissa Molina. The historical context is about the Rockaways. After Hurricane Sandy, the community felt like it was drowning. But stars rise. The students painted themselves as stars, rising from the ocean and shining over the beach. The mural at 2-45 Beach 79th Street is a constellation. When you look at it, you are seeing that even after the storm, the stars come out.

Unidos was created at the Borinquen Plaza Senior Center in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, in 2017 by artist Marissa Molina. The historical context is about the Puerto Rican community. Unidos means united. The senior center is a gathering place for elders who came from the island generations ago. Molina painted flags, flowers, and faces of young and old standing together. The mural at 80 Seigel Street is a family reunion. When you look at it, you are hearing Spanish and English mixing. Unidos. Together.

Creator was painted at Movement Day NYC in 2017 by Marissa Molina and Nico Collazo. The historical context is about faith and creativity. The conference brought together Christian leaders from around the city. The artists painted God's hands shaping the world, with tools like paintbrushes, hammers, and gardening spades. The mural at 2-26 East 120th Street is a theology lesson. When you look at it, you are learning that to be made in God's image is to be a creator. So create.

Welcome to PS 310 in Marble Hill, Bronx, was created in 2017 by Naomi Kuo and Pilar Batista. The historical context is about a neighborhood that is geographically Manhattan but culturally the Bronx. Marble Hill is confusing, but the welcome is clear. The artists painted a bright and friendly entrance scene, with flowers, children, and the words "Welcome to PS 310." The mural at 260 West Kingsbridge Road is a handshake. When you walk through the doors, you are being greeted. You belong here.

column6: Naomi Kuo, Pilar Batista, Jason "Obe" Martin
column13: IS 117X in Mount Hope, Bronx, got a mural in 2017 called "Celebrate Diversity," created by Naomi Kuo, Pilar Batista, and Jason "Obe" Martin. The historical context is about the multicultural makeup of Mount Hope. The school has students from the Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico, West Africa, and everywhere in between. The artists painted flags, faces, and foods from around the world. The mural at 1865 Morris Avenue is a festival. When you look at it, you are celebrating that different is not a problem. Different is beautiful.

Dream Walls 2.0 came to PS/MS 34 on the Lower East Side in 2017, nearly a decade after the original Dream Walls project. The first of five murals was "Be the Change," created by Nico Collazo and Jeremy Del Rio. The historical context is about the famous Gandhi quote. "Be the change you wish to see in the world." The students painted themselves as change makers, picking up trash, helping the elderly, and standing up to bullies. The mural at 730 East 12th Street is a challenge. When you look at it, you are being asked to stop waiting for someone else to fix the world. Be the change.

The second Dream Walls 2.0 mural was "Creativity," created by Nico Collazo and Jeremy Del Rio. The historical context is about the original 2007 mural of the same name. The students revisited the theme, painting images of artists, musicians, and writers at work. The mural at 730 East 12th Street is a sequel. When you look at it, you are seeing that creativity never gets old. It just gets reinvented.

The third Dream Walls 2.0 mural was "Dream Big," created by Nico Collazo and Jeremy Del Rio. The historical context is about the power of a dream. The students painted themselves dreaming of college, careers, and families. Some dreams were small. Some were huge. But all of them were valid. The mural at 730 East 12th Street is a permission slip. When you look at it, you are being told to dream as big as you want. No dream is too big.

The fourth Dream Walls 2.0 mural was "Opportunity," created by Nico Collazo and Jeremy Del Rio. The historical context is about the 2007 mural of the same name. The students explored what opportunity means today. A good school. A safe home. A fair chance. The mural at 730 East 12th Street is a definition. When you look at it, you are learning that opportunity is not luck. It is something you create and something you give.

The fifth Dream Walls 2.0 mural was "Xpress," created by Nico Collazo and Jeremy Del Rio. The historical context is about the 2007 mural of the same name. The students painted themselves expressing their identities, their feelings, and their dreams. The mural at 730 East 12th Street is a journal. When you look at it, you are reading the inner lives of young people. Xpress yourself.

Grand Street Campus in East Williamsburg, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2017 called "Rooted," created by Peach Tao and Nico Collazo. The historical context is about the school's diverse population. Students come from all over the world, but they are rooted in this building. The artists painted trees with roots that looked like family trees, showing the many countries represented. The mural at 850 Grand Street is a forest. When you look at it, you are seeing that roots can be in many places. But they all lead to the same tree.

Sierra High School in Azusa, California, got a mural in 2017 called "ImPossible," created by Ritchie Kong and Ronnie Robles. The historical context is about the power of belief. Impossible is just "I'm possible" with an apostrophe. The students painted themselves achieving things that seemed impossible, like graduating, going to college, and breaking cycles of poverty. The mural at 140 East Palm Drive is a magic trick. When you look at it, you are learning that impossible is just a word. Change the punctuation, change your life.

Create! Harlem was painted at Templo Biblico in Harlem in 2017 by artist Sam Wisneski. The historical context is about the intersection of faith and art. The church wanted to remind its congregation that creating is a spiritual act. Wisneski painted hands making things, paintbrushes, hammers, keyboards, and the word CREATE in bold letters. The mural at 503 West 126th Street is a commandment. When you look at it, you are being told to make something. Anything. Just create.

La Lucha Continua was painted at First Street Green Art Park in the East Village in 2017 by artist Sam Wisneski. The historical context is about activism. La Lucha Continua means "the struggle continues." The mural honored the activists who fought for workers' rights, immigrant rights, and racial justice. The artists painted portraits of heroes alongside blank spaces for future heroes to add their names. The mural at 33 East 1st Street is a protest sign. When you look at it, you are being told that the fight is not over. La lucha continua.

column1: Dance. Thrive. Chill. x Burton NYC
column6: Sam Wisneski, Nico Collazo, Michela Muserra, Marissa Molina
column13: Dance. Thrive. Chill. was created at the Burton Store in SoHo, Manhattan, in 2017 by Sam Wisneski, Nico Collazo, Michela Muserra, and Marissa Molina. The historical context is about snowboarding and culture. Burton is a snowboarding brand, and the store wanted a mural that captured the energy of winter sports. The artists painted dancers, snowboarders, and people chilling, all in bright, vibrant colors. The mural at 69 Greene Street is a mountain. When you look at it, you are feeling the rush of a downhill run. Dance. Thrive. Chill.

column1: PS 185K: See Yourself in the Story
column6: Andrea Amanda, Michela Mussera, Kristen Leung
column13: PS 185K in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, originally got a mural in 2018 called "See Yourself in the Story," created by Andrea Amanda, Michela Mussera, and Kristen Leung. The historical context is about representation. Every child deserves to see themselves reflected in the art on their school walls. The artists painted scenes from classic children's books, but with characters who looked like the students at PS 185. The mural at 8601 Ridge Boulevard was a mirror. In 2024, after prolonged building construction caused extensive damage, Andrea Amanda led a restoration of the piece. When you look at it today, you are seeing that some stories are worth telling twice.

PS 250 in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2018 called "The Places You'll Go," created by artist Chris Gomez. The historical context is about Dr. Seuss. The title is borrowed from the famous graduation book. Gomez painted students traveling to fantastical places, riding hot air balloons, sailing ships, and flying through space. The mural at 86 Montrose Avenue is a map. When you look at it, you are being told that your future is wide open. The places you will go are endless.

column6: Ivan Rodriguez, Irie Sesma, Jordan Clark
column13: San Diego's Mosaic was created at One San Diego in National City, California, in 2018 by artists Ivan Rodriguez, Irie Sesma, and Jordan Clark. The historical context is about the diversity of San Diego. The region is a mosaic of different cultures, races, and backgrounds. The artists painted a giant mosaic portrait made of tiny tiles, each tile representing a different community member. The mural at 710 East 16th Street is a group photo. When you look at it, you are seeing that everyone is a piece of the puzzle. Together, they make something beautiful.

Do You Love It? was painted at Thrive HQ in Manhattan's Civic Center in 2018 by artist Kekoa. The historical context is about passion. The question is simple but profound. Do you love what you do? Kekoa painted figures dancing, painting, and playing music, their faces full of joy. The mural is a test. When you look at it, you are being asked to answer honestly. If the answer is no, it is time to change something.

column10: 124th St & Malcolm X Blvd, New York, NY 10027
column13: Harlem Hub at the Living Redemption Youth Opportunity Hub in Harlem got a mural in 2018 called "Harlem Hub," created by artist Kekoa. The historical context is about the youth center itself. The Hub provides jobs, training, and mentoring for young people in Harlem. Kekoa painted portraits of students working, learning, and laughing together. The mural at 124th Street and Malcolm X Boulevard is a yearbook. When you look at it, you are seeing the faces of hope. This is the Harlem Hub.

column10: 200 Central Park W, New York, NY 10024
column13: Advancing Together X MCCA was created at the American Museum of Natural History on the Upper West Side in 2018 by artists Kekoa and Kristen Leung. The historical context is about partnership. The museum partnered with Thrive to create a mural celebrating diversity in science. The artists painted scientists of all races, genders, and backgrounds, working together to understand the natural world. The mural at 200 Central Park West is a laboratory. When you look at it, you are seeing that science is for everyone. Advancing together is the only way forward.

column10: 645 St. Nicholas Ave, New York, NY 10030
column13: For One and All was painted at the Harlem Hub Summer Arts Academy in Harlem in 2018 by Kekoa and Mario Ruiz. The historical context is about justice. The title comes from the phrase "justice for one is justice for all." The artists painted scales of justice, broken chains, and hands reaching for freedom. The mural at 645 St. Nicholas Avenue is a courtroom. When you look at it, you are being reminded that until everyone is free, no one is truly free.

column10: 124th St & Malcolm X Blvd, New York, NY 10027
column13: Do You Love It 2.0 was a sequel mural at the Living Redemption Youth Opportunity Hub in Harlem in 2018, created by Kekoa and Nico Collazo. The historical context is about the sequel being better than the original. The first Do You Love It? asked the question. The sequel helps you find the answer. The artists painted tools, mentors, and opportunities. The mural at 124th Street and Malcolm X Boulevard is a career fair. When you look at it, you are being shown how to find work you love. Do you love it? If not, here is how to change that.

Jill Chaifetz Transfer High School in Melrose, Bronx, got a mural in 2018 called "Every Journey," created by artist Marissa Molina. The historical context is about transfer schools. Jill Chaifetz serves students who have faced obstacles, homelessness, pregnancy, incarceration, or mental health struggles. Every journey looks different. Molina painted winding roads, each one unique, but all leading to the same destination, a diploma. The mural at 660 West 237th Street is a map. When you look at it, you are seeing that there is no wrong path. Only your path.

PS/MS 183Q in Arverne, Queens, got a mural in 2018 called "Your Best Self," created by artist Marissa Molina. The historical context is about growth. The students explored what it means to be your best self. Kind, honest, hardworking, and compassionate. Molina painted students as superheroes, but the superpowers were everyday virtues. The mural at 2-45 Beach 79th Street in Rockaway Beach is a mirror. When you look at it, you are being asked to look at yourself. Are you being your best self today?

PS/MS 42Q in Arverne, Queens, got a mural in 2018 called "Choose Kindness," created by artist Marissa Molina. The historical context is about the power of choice. Every day, you choose how to treat people. The students wanted a reminder to choose kindness. Molina painted hands helping, faces smiling, and the words "Choose Kindness" in bold letters. The mural at 488 Beach 66th Street is a decision. When you look at it, you are being asked to make the choice. Choose kindness.

MS 83X in Morris Park, Bronx, got a mural in 2018 called "Get Active," created by Marissa Molina and Stephen Uhey. The historical context is about health and fitness. The students explored what it means to be active, physically and mentally. The artists painted students playing sports, dancing, and even doing jumping jacks in the hallway. The mural at 950 Rhinelander Avenue is a gym class. When you look at it, you are being told to get up and move. Your body will thank you.

MS/HS 141, the Riverdale Kingsbridge Academy in Riverdale, Bronx, got a mural in 2018 called "One Tiger, Many Stripes," created by artist Marissa Molissa with help from student Rosabella. The historical context is about the school mascot and the diversity of the student body. Every tiger has stripes, but no two tigers have the same pattern. The artists painted tigers with stripes that looked like flags, maps, and family trees. The mural at 660 West 237th Street is a biology lesson. When you look at it, you are learning that unity does not mean sameness. One tiger, many stripes.

Dare Greatly was painted at PS 280Q in Jackson Heights, Queens, in 2018 by Michela Muserra and Pilar Batista. The historical context is about courage. The title is a quote from Theodore Roosevelt. "Far better it is to dare mighty things." The artists painted students taking risks, trying new things, and failing forward. The mural at 34-20 94th Street is a challenge. When you look at it, you are being dared to be great. Do not play small. Dare greatly.

column2: High School of Telecommunication Arts and Technology
column13: HSTAT, the High School of Telecommunication Arts and Technology in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2018 called "Migration Remix," created by Michela Mussera and Kristen Leung. The historical context is about immigration. The students come from families that migrated to New York from all over the world. The artists painted birds flying, ships sailing, and suitcases packed with dreams. The mural at 350 67th Street is a passport. When you look at it, you are seeing that migration is not a threat. It is a remix. Everyone adds their own verse.

column1: PS 185: See Yourself in the Story
column13: PS 185 in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, got another mural in 2018 also called "See Yourself in the Story," created by Michela Mussera and Kristen Leung. This was the original version before Andrea Amanda restored it in 2024. The historical context is the same. Representation matters. The artists painted fairy tale characters, but with a twist. The princess was a student from PS 185. The knight was a student from PS 185. The dragon was a student from PS 185. The mural at 8601 Ridge Boulevard was a dream. When you looked at it, you saw yourself in the story.

Superpowers & Serve with Heart was painted at PS 280Q in Jackson Heights, Queens, in 2018 by Michela Mussera and Pilar Batista. The historical context is about service. The students explored what it means to serve others with heart. The artists painted superheroes whose powers were helping, listening, and caring. The mural at 34-20 94th Street is a job description. When you look at it, you are learning that the best superpower is a serving heart.

The Beat of our Drums was created at Carnegie Hall in Hell's Kitchen, Manhattan, in 2018 by Michela Mussera and Pilar Batista. The historical context is about music. Carnegie Hall is one of the most famous concert venues in the world. The students explored the role of drums in different cultures, African djembe, Latin timbales, and Japanese taiko. The mural at 881 7th Avenue is a rhythm section. When you look at it, you can hear the beat. The beat of our drums.

PS 327 in Brownsville, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2018 called "Soaring High," created by Peach Tao and Nico Colazzo. The historical context is about a neighborhood that is often defined by its challenges. Brownsville has high poverty and high crime, but it also has high hopes. The artists painted students as eagles, flying above the buildings and the statistics. The mural at 111 Bristol Street is a flight pattern. When you look at it, you are soaring. Do not look down.

Walton Campus in Kingsbridge Heights, Bronx, got a mural in 2018 called "The World We Make," created by Peach Tao and Nico Collazo. The historical context is about creation. The world is not something we inherit. It is something we make. The artists painted students building the world with their bare hands, shaping mountains, planting forests, and painting sunsets. The mural at 2780 Reservoir Avenue is a construction site. When you look at it, you are being told to pick up a tool. The world we make starts now.

Harlem Hub got another mural in 2018 called "Map It," created by Sally Sasz and Chloe Pitkoff. The historical context is about planning for the future. The students at Harlem Hub are learning to map out their lives, setting goals and figuring out how to reach them. The artists painted maps, compasses, and GPS coordinates. The mural at 260 West 40th Street is a navigation system. When you look at it, you are being told to map it. You cannot get where you are going without a plan.

column10: 124th St & Malcolm X Blvd, New York, NY 10027
column13: Beautifully x AC Hotel was created at the AC Hotel Times Square in the Garment District in 2018 by Sam Wisneski and Kekoa. The historical context is about hotel art. The hotel wanted a mural that would welcome guests and make them feel the energy of New York. The artists painted the word "Beautifully" in elegant script, surrounded by images of the city. The mural at 124th Street and Malcolm X Boulevard is a first impression. When you look at it, you are being told that New York is beautifully chaotic, beautifully diverse, beautifully alive.

IS 123X in Soundview, Bronx, got two murals in 2018. The first was "I Am the Bronx," created by the legendary graffiti crew TATS Cru along with Nico Collazo. The historical context is about Bronx pride. The Bronx is often disrespected, but the students wanted to shout their identity. The artists painted the words "I Am the Bronx" in bold graffiti style, surrounded by Bronx icons like Yankee Stadium, the Grand Concourse, and the Hip Hop sign. The mural at 260 West 40th Street is a declaration. When you look at it, you are hearing a roar. I am the Bronx.

The second IS 123X mural was "Bronx Legacy," created by Toofly and Nico Collazo. The historical context is about the artists and activists who came from the Bronx. The students painted portraits of heroes like Jennifer Lopez, Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor, and hip hop pioneer DJ Kool Herc. The mural at 1645 Commonwealth Avenue is a family tree. When you look at it, you are seeing that the Bronx has given the world so much. Now it is your turn to add to the legacy.

column1: 0 Bring Art Back: Mott Haven Collection Summer Intensive (Bronx 2018) More Details
column6: William Acevedo, John "Crash" Matos, TatsCru, Bio, Nicer, BG183, Jon143, BR162, Marissa Molina
column13: Bring Art Back: Mott Haven Collection was a Summer Intensive project in Mott Haven, Bronx, in 2018, created by a massive team including William Acevedo, John "Crash" Matos, TatsCru, Bio, Nicer, BG183, Jon143, BR162, and Marissa Molina. The historical context is about art as a right, not a luxury. The students and professional artists worked together to create multiple murals throughout the neighborhood. The collection at 1645 Commonwealth Avenue is a museum without walls. When you walk through Mott Haven, you are seeing that art belongs to everyone.

column10: Major Deegan Expressway & E 138th St, Bronx, NY 10454
column13: Make Space for the Arts was a massive community mural collaboration on the Major Deegan Expressway in Mott Haven, Bronx, in 2018, created by William Acevedo, TatsCru, Crash, Bio, Nicer, BG183, Jon143, BR162, and Marissa Molina. The historical context is about reclaiming public space. The underpass of the Major Deegan Expressway is dark, loud, and ugly. But the artists transformed it into a gallery. Over 2,000 square feet of public art covered both sides of the underpass at Alexander Avenue and 135th Street. The project involved eighteen students and dozens of volunteers from Viacom, Kenneth Cole, and Resurrection Church. The mural was featured on NY1 and NY1 Noticias. When you look at it, you are seeing that even the most neglected corners of a city can be made beautiful. Make space for the arts. Always.

PS/IS 30 in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, got two murals in 2019. The first was "Opportunity," created by Abby Walsh and Nico Collazo in the arts and sciences wing. The historical context is about the school's location and the long arc of Thrive Collective's work. The mural celebrates how creative imagination opens the doors of opportunity, and how the arts and sciences unlock that imagination. For Thrive, this project felt like a homecoming. In 2011, Thrive's creative director Sam Wisneski directed his first school mural at PS 102 in Bay Ridge, and IS 30's art teacher Mr. David Askew brought students from PS/IS 30 to volunteer on Saturdays that spring. Eight years later, Council Member Justin Brannan funded Thrive to work with PS/IS 30 students. The mural at Foley Square is actually mislocated, but the spirit is clear. Opportunity is not luck. It is a door. The arts and sciences hold the key.

column1: Ember Charter School: The Fabric of Leadership
column13: Ember Charter School in Bed Stuy, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2019 called "The Fabric of Leadership," created by Abby Walsh and Will DeNatale. The historical context is about the school's mission to train young leaders. The artists asked students what leadership was made of. The answers became the fabric of the mural. Courage, honesty, empathy, and vision. The artists painted these qualities as threads woven together into a colorful tapestry. The mural at 616 Quincy Street is a loom. When you look at it, you are seeing that leadership is not one thing. It is many things, woven together into something strong.

MS 83X in Morris Park, Bronx, got a mural in 2019 called "Respect Road," created by Breana Vazquez and Peach Tao. The historical context is about the school's values. Respect is not just a word. It is a road you walk every day. The artists painted a winding road with signposts marking different kinds of respect. Respect yourself. Respect others. Respect your community. Respect your environment. The mural at 950 Rhinelander Avenue is a path. When you look at it, you are being asked which way you will go. Respect road starts here.

Hope Oakland was created at the UrbanLife Youth & Family Center in West Oakland's Lower Bottoms neighborhood in 2019 by artists Camer1 and Tim. The historical context is about a community that has been systematically neglected. The Lower Bottoms has high poverty and high crime, but it also has hope. The artists painted the word HOPE in large letters, surrounded by images of young people laughing, studying, and playing. The mural at 1800 Campbell Street is a sunrise. When you look at it, you are seeing that even in the darkest place, hope lives.

The "Roots/Raíces" Series was a collection of murals at the NYCHA Lillian Wald Senior Center on the Lower East Side in 2019, all created by artist Fermin Mendoza. The first was "Alphabet City." The historical context is about the neighborhood's nickname. Alphabet City is named for Avenues A, B, C, and D. The artists painted the letters of the alphabet intertwined with images of the neighborhood's history, from tenements to community gardens. The mural at 12 Avenue D is a dictionary. When you look at it, you are learning to read the neighborhood.

The second Roots/Raíces mural was "Coquí." The historical context is about Puerto Rican culture. The coquí is a tiny frog native to Puerto Rico, and its call is a beloved sound of the island. The artists painted coquí frogs alongside the words "Raíces" meaning roots. The mural at 12 Avenue D is a song. When you look at it, you can almost hear the coquí calling. It is the sound of home.

The third Roots/Raíces mural was "Flor de Maga." The historical context is about the national flower of Puerto Rico. The Flor de Maga is a bright pink flower that represents resilience and beauty. The artists painted the flower in full bloom, alongside images of the island's mountains and coastlines. The mural at 12 Avenue D is a garden. When you look at it, you are seeing that even in New York, Puerto Rico blooms.

MS/HS 141, the Riverdale Kingsbridge Academy in Riverdale, Bronx, got a mural in 2019 called "Celebrate Diversity," created by artist Fermin Mendoza. The historical context is about the school's diverse student body. Students come from families all over the world. The artists painted flags, faces, and traditional clothing from the many countries represented. The mural at 660 West 237th Street is a festival. When you look at it, you are celebrating that different is beautiful.

The fourth Roots/Raíces mural was "Capicu." The historical context is about Puerto Rican slang. Capicu is a term used in the game of dominoes, meaning the game is over. But it also means the end of something, and the beginning of something else. The artists painted dominoes falling, with the word "Capicu" in bold letters. The mural at 12 Avenue D is a game. When you look at it, you are learning that every ending is also a beginning.

The fifth Roots/Raíces mural was "Piraguas." The historical context is about a traditional Puerto Rican treat. Piraguas are shaved ice with flavored syrup, sold from pushcarts on the island and in New York. The artists painted a piragua cart, with colorful syrups and a smiling vendor. The mural at 12 Avenue D is a memory. When you look at it, you can taste the sweet, cold treat on a hot summer day.

The Work of our Hands was created at Connect Life Church in Flatbush, Brooklyn, in 2019 by Jon Souza and Breana Vazquez. The historical context is about faith in action. The church wanted to remind its congregation that faith without works is dead. The artists painted hands building, healing, teaching, and praying. The mural at 249 East 17th Street is a mission statement. When you look at it, you are being asked what your hands will do today.

PS/IS 30's second mural was "Resilience," created by Joshua Gabriel and Nico Collazo outside the gym. The historical context is about bouncing back. The students explored what it means to fall down and get back up. The artists painted athletes falling and rising, students failing tests and studying harder, and families facing hardship and staying together. The mural at 1215 81st Street in Brooklyn is a muscle. When you look at it, you are being told that resilience is like a muscle. You have to exercise it to make it strong.

The UrbanLife Youth & Family Center in West Oakland got another mural in 2019 created by Kekoa, Camer1, and Tim. This one focused on the center's mission to serve young people. The artists painted students working on computers, playing sports, and receiving mentoring. The mural at 1800 Campbell Street is a brochure. When you look at it, you are seeing what UrbanLife offers. Hope, opportunity, and love.

Edition Times Square Hotel in the Theater District, Manhattan, got four murals in 2019 created by Kekoa and Kristen Leung. The first was "Authenticity." The historical context is about being real in a city of fakes. Times Square is full of tourists, cartoons, and cheap souvenirs. The artists painted the word "Authenticity" alongside images of real New Yorkers, the people who actually live and work in the city. The mural at 20 Times Square is a truth serum. When you look at it, you are being asked to be yourself. Not a copy.

The second Edition mural was "Enchantment." The historical context is about the magic of New York. Even in the chaos of Times Square, there is enchantment. The artists painted stars, sparkling lights, and figures caught in a moment of wonder. The mural at 20 Times Square is a spell. When you look at it, you are feeling the magic of the city.

The third Edition mural was "Passion." The historical context is about the drive that makes New Yorkers work so hard. The artists painted people lost in their passions, dancing, painting, cooking, and coding. The mural at 20 Times Square is a fire. When you look at it, you are feeling the heat of people who love what they do.

The fourth Edition mural was "Sophistication." The historical context is about the elegance of New York. The city is not just loud and fast. It is also sophisticated. The artists painted tuxedos, evening gowns, and the skyline at sunset. The mural at 20 Times Square is a cocktail party. When you look at it, you are dressing up and going out. That is sophistication.

PS/MS 42Q in Arverne, Queens, got a mural in 2019 called "Anything is Possible," created by artist Marissa Molina. The historical context is about the Rockaways. After Hurricane Sandy, the community felt like nothing was possible. But by 2019, they had rebuilt. The students wanted a reminder that anything is possible. Molina painted students flying, swimming, and climbing mountains. The mural at 488 Beach 66th Street is a dare. When you look at it, you are being told to try the impossible. Because anything is possible.

column1: The Mayor's Fund for NYC 25th Anniversary Gala
column7: Victoria Cruz, Christopher Ajayi, Rosabella Garcia, Judah Del Rio
column10: E 88th St & East End Ave, New York, NY 10128
column13: The Mayor's Fund for NYC 25th Anniversary Gala at Gracie Mansion on the Upper East Side featured a live painting by Marissa Molina, with help from Victoria Cruz, Christopher Ajayi, Rosabella Garcia, and Judah Del Rio in 2019. The historical context is about philanthropy. The Mayor's Fund supports programs that help New Yorkers in need. The artists painted a colorful, abstract celebration of the city's diversity and resilience. The mural at East 88th Street and East End Avenue was a birthday cake. When you looked at it, you were celebrating 25 years of giving back.

BCMS/PS 298 at the Betty Shabazz Campus in Brownsville, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2019 called "Live Well," created by Marissa Molina and Nico Collazo. The historical context is about health and wellness. Brownsville has high rates of asthma, diabetes, and obesity. The students wanted a reminder to live well. The artists painted fruits, vegetables, exercise, and sleep. The mural at 300 Chester Street is a doctor's note. When you look at it, you are being prescribed a healthy life.

PS 102 in Bay Ridge got a "Welcome Refresh" mural in 2019, created by Marissa Molina and Peach Tao. The historical context is about the original 2011 Welcome mural. Eight years later, the mural needed a refresh. The artists updated the languages, added new faces, and brightened the colors. The mural at 211 72nd Street is a software update. When you look at it, you are seeing that welcome never gets old. But it does need a refresh sometimes.

column6: Marissa Molina, Peach Tao, Will DeNatale
column13: Tree of Life was created at First Presbyterian Church of Jamaica in Queens in 2019 by Marissa Molina, Peach Tao, and Will DeNatale. The historical context is about the church's congregation. The members came from many different backgrounds, but they were all part of the same tree. The artists painted a giant tree with roots that looked like family trees and branches that held the flags of many nations. The mural at 89-60 164th Street is a sanctuary. When you look at it, you are sitting under the tree. Feel the shade. Feel the belonging.

column10: 442 E Houston St, New York, NY 10002
column13: Islanders Dive Deeper was created at PS 188 The Island School on the Lower East Side in 2019 by Marissa Molina and Romero Britto, featuring SpongeBob SquarePants. The historical context is about the New York Islanders hockey team. The Islanders partnered with Thrive to create a mural encouraging students to "dive deeper" into their education. The artists painted SpongeBob, Patrick, and other characters studying, reading, and playing hockey. The mural at 442 East Houston Street is a cartoon. When you look at it, you are laughing and learning at the same time.

MS 183Q in Arverne, Queens, got a mural in 2019 called "Yes I Can," created by Marissa Molina and Will DeNatale. The historical context is about self belief. The students explored the power of saying "yes I can" instead of "no I can't." The artists painted students overcoming obstacles, climbing walls, and breaking through ceilings. The mural at 2-45 Beach 79th Street is a mantra. When you look at it, you are being told to say the words out loud. Yes I can.

column10: Mt Morris Park West & W 124th St, New York, NY 10027
column13: Thoughts and Prayers was created at the Art of Healing Harlem Festival in 2019 by Marissa Molina and Will DeNatale. The historical context is about the phrase "thoughts and prayers" after gun violence. The artists wanted to move beyond thoughts and prayers to action. They painted hands doing things, writing letters to politicians, voting, and protesting. The mural at Mt Morris Park West and West 124th Street is a call to action. When you look at it, you are being told that thoughts and prayers are not enough. Do something.

Welcome: You Belong Here was painted at PS 280Q in Jackson Heights, Queens, in 2019 by Marissa Molina and Will DeNatale. The historical context is about the most diverse neighborhood in the world. Jackson Heights has families from over 100 countries. The artists painted the words "You Belong Here" in multiple languages, surrounded by open doors and smiling faces. The mural at 34-20 94th Street is a hug. When you look at it, you are being welcomed. No matter where you are from. You belong here.

Serendipity was created at PS 282 Elementary School in Park Slope, Brooklyn, in 2019 by artist Michela Muserra. The historical context is about happy accidents. Serendipity is finding something wonderful without looking for it. The artists painted students making unexpected discoveries, like finding a book they love or making a new friend. The mural at 180 6th Avenue is a lucky charm. When you look at it, you are hoping for serendipity. But you are also learning that you have to be open to it.

PS 204K in Bensonhurst, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2019 called "The Games We Play," created by Michela Muserra and Abby Walsh. The historical context is about play. The students explored the games they play at school and at home. Board games, video games, sports, and imagination games. The artists painted children playing chess, tag, and make believe. The mural at 1301 66th Street is a game manual. When you look at it, you are learning that play is not a waste of time. Play is how you learn to win, lose, and get along.

PS 280Q got another mural in 2019 called "It Takes a Village," created by Michela Mussera and Breanna Vazquez. The historical context is about the African proverb. It takes a village to raise a child. The artists painted the village, parents, teachers, coaches, and neighbors all surrounding a group of children. The mural at 34-20 94th Street is a family photo. When you look at it, you are seeing the village that raised you. Thank them.

Tiger Pride was created at MS/HS 141 in Riverdale, Bronx, in 2019 by artist Nico Collazo. The historical context is about the school mascot. The tiger represents strength, courage, and pride. Collazo painted a giant tiger with the eyes of students, the stripes of different cultures, and the heart of the community. The mural at 660 West 237th Street is a roar. When you look at it, you are hearing the school cheer. Tiger pride.

Youth Day Festivals in Mott Haven, Bronx, got a mural in 2019 called "Hopes and Dreams," created by artist Nico Collazo. The historical context is about the dreams of young people. The artists asked students what they hoped for. The answers became the mural. College, careers, families, peace, and joy. The mural at 340 East 138th Street is a wish list. When you look at it, you are reading the hopes of a generation. Do not let them down.

PS 245K in Flatbush, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2019 called "Creators," created by artist Peach Tao. The historical context is about the power to make things. Every student is a creator. The artists painted students making art, music, writing, and inventions. The mural at 1780 Ocean Avenue is a factory. When you look at it, you are seeing that you do not have to be a consumer. You can be a creator.

Discovery HS in Kingsbridge Heights, Bronx, got a four mural series in 2019 called "Cognition Series," created by Peach Tao and Chris Gomez. The first mural showed puzzle pieces coming together. The historical context is about how the brain solves problems. The mural at 2780 Reservoir Avenue is a brain teaser. When you look at it, you are putting the pieces together.
The second Cognition mural showed a light bulb turning on. The mural at 2780 Reservoir Avenue is an idea. When you look at it, you are seeing the moment of discovery.
The third Cognition mural showed a network of neurons firing. The mural at 2780 Reservoir Avenue is a brain scan. When you look at it, you are watching your brain work.

The fourth Cognition mural showed a student having an "aha" moment. The murals at 2780 Reservoir Avenue are a brain scan. When you look at them, you are seeing how thinking works. Cognition is the most beautiful thing in the universe.

Walton Campus in Kingsbridge Heights, Bronx, got a mural in 2019 called "Global Gastronomy," created by Peach Tao and Chris Gomez. The historical context is about food and culture. The students came from families all over the world, and they wanted to celebrate the foods of their heritage. The artists painted dishes from Italy, China, Mexico, and Ghana. The mural at 2780 Reservoir Avenue is a menu. When you look at it, you are getting hungry. Hungry for food. Hungry for culture.

Kids Comic Con 2019 in Civic Center, Manhattan, got a mural called "Team Titans," created by artist Sam Wisneski. The historical context is about comics and collaboration. The artists worked with young comic book fans to create a superhero team. Each student designed their own hero, and Wisneski wove them into a single epic scene. The mural is a comic book cover. When you look at it, you are seeing that everyone can be a hero. You just need a team.

Los Tapatios in Paradise Hills, San Diego, got a mural in 2019 called "Reo Drive Flowers," created by artist Selina Calvo. The historical context is about a Mexican restaurant that serves the community. The owners wanted to celebrate the beauty of their culture. Calvo painted bright flowers, cacti, and colorful patterns. The mural at 2335 Reo Drive is a garden. When you look at it, you are smelling the flowers and tasting the food. Los Tapatios is home.

Judith Kaye High School in South Ozone Park, Queens, got a mural in 2019 called "Undeterred," created by Toofly and Pilar Batista with a student named Natalie who was a self taught artist. The historical context is about the school's name. Judith Kaye was the first female chief judge of the New York Court of Appeals. She was undeterred by the obstacles in her path. The students designed the concept around the word "Undeterred," with a central portrait of a student (Natalie's design) who refuses to quit. The mural at 158-40 102nd Street is a biography. When you look at it, you are reading the story of a judge who never gave up. And the students who follow in her footsteps. Undeterred.

MS 183Q in Arverne, Queens, got a mural in 2019 called "Harmony," created by Will DeNatale. The historical context is about the different elements of the school community coming together. DeNatale painted musical notes, colors, and shapes all working together in harmony. The mural at 2-45 Beach 79th Street is a chord. When you look at it, you are hearing harmony.

PS 163 in Bath Beach, Brooklyn, got a three mural series in 2020 called "United We Play," created by artist Abby Walsh. The historical context is about the pandemic. 2020 was the year COVID-19 shut down schools, playgrounds, and sports. Children were stuck inside, lonely and bored. Walsh painted children playing together, jumping rope, playing tag, and swinging on swings. The first mural at 109 Bay 14th Street shows kids in a park. When you look at it, you are seeing what every child lost in 2020, and what they desperately wanted back. United we play. Separate, we suffer.

The second mural in the "United We Play" series at PS 163 shows children playing in a schoolyard, running, laughing, and competing in friendly games. The mural at 109 Bay 14th Street is a memory of normalcy. When you look at it, you are reminded of the joy of recess.

The third mural in the "United We Play" series at PS 163 shows children in a fantasy world of imagination, playing with imaginary friends and creating games out of nothing. The mural at 109 Bay 14th Street is a dream. When you look at it, you are seeing that even when stuck inside, children can still play with their imaginations.

The Importance of Daydreaming was created at IS 117 and The Young Women's Leadership School in Mount Hope, Bronx, in 2020 by Abby Walsh and Nico Collazo. The historical context is about the pandemic's mental health toll. Students were stressed, anxious, and depressed. Daydreaming felt like a luxury they could not afford. But the artists argued the opposite. Daydreaming is essential. Walsh and Collazo painted students with their heads in the clouds, imagining futures, solving problems, and finding peace. The mural at 1865 Morris Avenue is a prescription. When you look at it, you are being told to let your mind wander. Daydreaming is not wasting time. It is survival.

column10: 1601 Morning Breeze Ln, National City, CA 91950
column13: Concrete & Canvas in National City, San Diego, got two murals in 2020 created by Angelina Deugan and Julio Olvera. The first was "Be Kind." The historical context is about the cruelty of the pandemic year. People were scared and angry. Kindness felt rare. The artists painted the words "Be Kind" in rainbow colors, surrounded by smiling faces and helping hands. The mural at 1601 Morning Breeze Lane is a reminder. When you look at it, you are being told that kindness costs nothing but means everything. Be kind.

column10: 1601 Morning Breeze Ln, National City, CA 91950
column13: The second Concrete & Canvas mural was "She Is." The historical context is about honoring women, especially women of color who were on the front lines of the pandemic as nurses, teachers, and essential workers. The artists painted portraits of strong women, mothers, daughters, and grandmothers, with the words "She Is" followed by adjectives like brave, beautiful, and brilliant. The mural at the same address is a tribute. When you look at it, you are seeing that she is everything.

Thrive Customs was painted at the East Harlem Ministry Hub in 2020 by artist Carmen Sanchez. The historical context is about the resilience of East Harlem. The neighborhood was hit hard by COVID, but the community kept fighting. Sanchez painted custom sneakers and clothing on the wall, a nod to the creativity of young people. The mural is a fashion show. When you look at it, you are seeing that even in a pandemic, style matters. Self expression matters.

The Work of Our Hands was created at Connect Life Church in Flatbush, Brooklyn, in 2020 by artist Jon Souza. The historical context is about faith during crisis. Churches were closed, but the work of faith continued. Souza painted hands doing various kinds of work, building, healing, teaching, and praying. The mural at 249 East 17th Street is a Bible verse. When you look at it, you are reading the words "May the favor of the Lord our God rest on us; establish the work of our hands for us."

Picture the world in the summer of 2020. The COVID quarantine had just lifted, and small businesses everywhere were struggling to find their footing. That year, Thrive Collective’s San Diego affiliate, Concrete & Canvas, brought together three local artists, karina @xkvrf, sophy @sketchbook.definition, and Miguel Zepeda, along with student volunteers, to paint something joyful on the walls of La Palapa Market, a beloved community market at 2335 Reo Drive in the Paradise Hills neighborhood of San Diego. They called their creation "Fiesta." Paradise Hills had deep roots as a blue collar neighborhood with a strong Navy presence and a vibrant Latinx community, a place where families had gathered for generations. As the artists painted, the mural became a quiet act of defiance against the fear and isolation of the pandemic. The bright colors and swirling patterns were a promise that the spirit of celebration could not be erased. For every neighbor who walked through those doors, "Fiesta" whispered a simple but powerful truth: after the hard times, there is always a reason to dance again.

Juarez Kajukenbo in Oakland, California, got a mural in 2020 created by Kekoa and Kristen Hubbard. The historical context is about martial arts and community. Kajukenbo is a mixed martial art that emphasizes self defense and discipline. The studio had been a safe haven for young people in Oakland for decades. The artists painted fighters in action, along with the values of the practice, respect, honor, and perseverance. The mural at 5680 San Pablo Avenue is a dojo. When you look at it, you are learning that the fight is not just physical. It is mental and spiritual too.

column2: Boerum Hill School of International Studies
column13: BHSIS, the Boerum Hill School of International Studies in Carroll Gardens, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2020 called "For One and All," created by artist Marissa Molina. The historical context is about the school's international focus. Students come from families all over the world. The artists painted flags, maps, and faces from every continent, with the words "For One and All" in the center. The mural at 284 Baltic Street is a passport. When you look at it, you are seeing that justice for one is justice for all. No matter where you are from.

Hope and Opportunity was painted on the floor of the East Harlem Ministry Hub in 2020 by artist Marissa Molina. The historical context is about the physical space of the hub. The floor was just concrete until Molina turned it into a canvas. She painted the words "Hope" and "Opportunity" in bright colors, surrounded by stars and arrows pointing forward. The floor mural is a foundation. When you walk on it, you are stepping on hope. Every step matters.

New York Strong was created at PS 155 William Paca School in East Harlem in 2020 by artist Marissa Molina. The historical context is about the phrase that defined the pandemic. "New York Strong" became a mantra for a city that was hit first and hit hardest. Molina painted the words in bold letters, surrounded by images of first responders, nurses, and everyday heroes. The mural at 319 East 117th Street is a flex. When you look at it, you are seeing that New York did not break. New York got stronger.

The Clemente Soto Velez Cultural Center on the Lower East Side got a mural in 2020 called "Arte Pa'Mi Gente," meaning Art for My People, created by Marissa Molina and Kekoa. The historical context is about the center's mission. The Clemente has been a home for Latino art for decades. The artists painted portraits of artists, musicians, and dancers, along with the words "Arte Pa'Mi Gente." The mural at 107 Suffolk Street is a manifesto. When you look at it, you are learning that art is not a luxury. Art is for the people.

column6: Marissa Molina, Nico Collazo, Rebecca Heritage
column13: Flowers of our People was painted at the NYCHA Stapleton Senior Center on Staten Island in 2020 by Marissa Molina, Nico Collazo, and Rebecca Heritage. The historical context is about the elders who raised the community. They are the flowers of our people. The artists painted portraits of seniors, their faces turned into flowers, blooming even in winter. The mural at 189 Gordon Street is a garden. When you look at it, you are honoring the elders who planted the seeds. Now it is your turn to water them.

PS/MS 42Q in Arverne, Queens, got a mural in 2020 called "The Tree of Peace," created by Marissa Molina and Will DeNatale. The historical context is about the Rockaways' recovery from Hurricane Sandy and the added trauma of the pandemic. The students needed peace. The artists painted a giant tree with roots that looked like family trees and branches that reached toward the sky. The mural at 488 Beach 66th Street is a sanctuary. When you look at it, you are sitting under the tree. Feel the shade. Feel the peace.

Do You Love It? was painted at the East Harlem Ministry Hub in 2020 by artist Michela Muserra. The historical context is about finding your passion. The question is simple but life changing. Muserra painted figures working at jobs they love, smiling, laughing, and thriving. The mural is a career fair. When you look at it, you are being asked the question. Do you love it? If not, keep searching.

The East Harlem Ministry Hub also got a namesake mural in 2020 created by Michela Muserra. The historical context is about the hub itself. The building at 237 East 104th Street is a beacon of hope in East Harlem. Muserra painted the words "East Harlem Ministry Hub" surrounded by images of the community, children, churches, and corner stores. The mural is a signpost. When you look at it, you are seeing that this place is holy ground.

column2: Union Settlement East Harlem Youth Opportunity Hub
column13: The Lamar Gibson Memorial was painted at the Union Settlement East Harlem Youth Opportunity Hub in 2020 by artist Michela Muserra. The historical context is about loss. Lamar Gibson was a young man from East Harlem who was killed by gun violence. Too young. Too soon. Muserra painted his portrait, along with angel wings and the words "Rest in Paradise." The mural at 237 East 104th Street is a funeral. When you look at it, you are mourning a life cut short. And you are promising to stop the violence that took him.

Little Lola and Tots in Brooklyn got a mural in 2020 created by artist Michela Muserra. The historical context is about early childhood education. Little Lola and Tots is a daycare and preschool. Muserra painted colorful animals, letters, and numbers, along with smiling children playing together. The mural is a classroom. When you look at it, you are seeing that learning starts early. And it should be fun.

PS 264K in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2020 called "Create," created by Michela Muserra and Abby Walsh. The historical context is about the creative process. The school wanted to encourage students to make things, not just consume them. The artists painted paintbrushes, musical notes, building blocks, and the word "Create" in bold letters. The mural is an invitation. When you look at it, you are being told to pick up a tool and make something. Anything. Just create.

A Wrinkle in Time was created at the Riverdale Kingsbridge Academy in Riverdale, Bronx, in 2020 by Nico Collazo and Cori Santana. The historical context is about the famous book by Madeleine L'Engle. The story is about traveling through space and time to save a father. The students related to the themes of loss, courage, and family. The artists painted the main characters, along with tessering, the method of time travel in the book. The mural at 1615 67th Street in Brooklyn is a book report. When you look at it, you are being reminded that love can bend time.

column2: Union Settlement East Harlem Youth Opportunity Hub
column13: RIP Lamar was another memorial mural for Lamar Gibson, this one at the Union Settlement East Harlem Youth Opportunity Hub, created by Nico Collazo and Michela Muserra in 2020. The historical context is the same. A young life lost too soon. This mural focused on Lamar's smile, his love of basketball, and his dream of graduating. The mural at 660 West 237th Street in the Bronx is a eulogy. When you look at it, you are hearing his name. Say it out loud. Lamar Gibson. Rest in power.

Blossoming was a three mural series at PS 249K in Flatbush, Brooklyn, created by artist Peach Tao in 2020. The historical context is about growth during hardship. 2020 was a year of lockdowns, but flowers still bloom. Tao painted flowers at different stages, seeds, sprouts, buds, and full blooms. The first mural shows a seed cracking open. The murals at 237 E 104th Street in Manhattan are mislocated, but the message is clear. Even in the worst year, you can still blossom.

The second mural in the "Blossoming" series at PS 249K shows a sprout reaching for the sun. The mural at 18 Marlborough Road is a hope. When you look at it, you are watching something new begin to grow.

The third mural in the "Blossoming" series at PS 249K shows a full flower in brilliant color. The mural at 18 Marlborough Road is a celebration. When you look at it, you are seeing that even in the worst year, you can still blossom.

Dragon Lion Medley was created for the Chinatown Mural Project in Manhattan in 2020 by artist Peach Tao. The historical context is about the rise in anti Asian hate during the pandemic. Chinatown was attacked, and the community was scared. The artists painted a dragon and a lion, traditional symbols of strength and protection in Chinese culture. The mural at 18 Marlborough Road in Brooklyn is a shield. When you look at it, you are seeing that Chinatown is not weak. Chinatown is powerful. The dragon and the lion protect their own.

Soaring Towards Excellence was painted at PS/IS 288 in Coney Island, Brooklyn, in 2020 by artist Peach Tao. The historical context is about the school's commitment to excellence despite the challenges of the pandemic. The students kept showing up, learning online, and doing their best. Tao painted students as eagles, flying high above the beach and the boardwalk. The mural at 140 E Broadway in Manhattan is a report card. When you look at it, you are seeing that excellence is not about perfect scores. It is about soaring when the wind is against you.

Bay Ridge Kindness was created at Lowen's Pharmacy in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, in 2020 by artists Toofly and Jon "Phes" Souza. The historical context is about small businesses during the pandemic. Pharmacies were essential, and Lowen's kept serving the community. The artists painted the words "Bay Ridge Kindness" along with images of hearts, masks, and thank you notes. The mural at 2950 West 25th Street in Brooklyn is a thank you card. When you look at it, you are thanking the pharmacists who risked their health to keep you healthy.

Kindness Beats the Virus was a two mural series in 2020. The first was at the Clemente Soto Velez Cultural Center on the Lower East Side, created by Toofly, Marissa Molina, and Kekoa. The historical context is about the pandemic. The virus was beating us, but kindness could beat the virus. The artists painted the phrase in bold letters, surrounded by masks, hand sanitizer, and social distancing circles. The mural at 6902 3rd Avenue in Brooklyn is a vaccine. When you look at it, you are learning that kindness is contagious too. Spread it.

The second Kindness Beats the Virus mural was at PS 155 in East Harlem, created by Toofly and Michela Muserra. The historical context is the same. The students needed to know that kindness was still possible, even when they could not hug their friends. The artists painted children waving from windows, sending hearts through screens, and leaving food on doorsteps. The mural at 107 Suffolk Street is a care package. When you look at it, you are being reminded that you can still be kind. Even from six feet away.

column6: WXY Studio, Tijay Mohammed, Sophia Dawson, Patrice Payne, Bio, Nicer, BG183, Crash, Andre Trenier, Eric Orr, Charlie Doves, Marth Alicia, Peter Paid, Giannina Gutierrez, Jamie Hef, SadeTCM, Sienide, Mark Lawrence, Key Detail, Jon “PHES” Souza, Marissa Molina, Peach Tao, Will DeNatale, Abby Walsh, Dax Matlock, Rebecca Heritage
column10: Lafayette Street Worth Street, Centre St, New York, NY 10013
column13: Black Lives Matter: A+ was a historic mural in Foley Square, Civic Center, Manhattan, created in July 2020 by an all star lineup of artists led by Tats Cru, with Thrive Collective artists including Jon "PHES" Souza, Marissa Molina, Peach Tao, Will DeNatale, Abby Walsh, Dax Matlock, and Rebecca Heritage. The historical context is the summer of racial justice protests after the murder of George Floyd. The mural spans three blocks on Centre Street in front of the federal and state courthouses. Thrive's primary assignment was the A in "Black." The A sits directly in front of the Thurgood Marshall nameplate on the federal courthouse. Marshall argued the landmark Brown v. Board of Education case that overturned Jim Crow and desegregated public schools. He later became the first Black Supreme Court justice. The mural at 319 E 117th Street is a history lesson. When you look at it, you are standing on holy ground. The A is for Abolition. The A is for Action. The A is for Always. Black Lives Matter. Today, tomorrow, and forever.

column2: Bronx School for Law, Government and Justice
column13: The Bronx School for Law, Government and Justice in Concourse Village got a mural in 2021 called "Champions of the Charge," created by Abby Walsh. The historical context is about the school's focus on law and justice. The students explored what it means to be a champion for justice. Walsh painted students as champions holding scales of justice, gavels, and law books. The mural at 244 E 163rd Street is a courtroom. When you look at it, you are seeing the champions of the charge.

IS 117 and The Young Women's Leadership School in Mount Hope, Bronx, got a mural in 2021 called "Pandemic Reflections," created by Abby Walsh. The historical context is about the COVID-19 pandemic and its impact on students. The students reflected on what they lost and what they learned. Walsh painted images of masks, Zoom screens, and empty streets, alongside symbols of hope like rainbows and hearts. The mural at 1865 Morris Avenue is a diary. When you look at it, you are reading pandemic reflections.

PS 280Q in Jackson Heights, Queens, got a mural in 2021 called "Home of the Lionhearts," created by Abby Walsh. The historical context is about the school's lion mascot and the bravery of the students during the pandemic. The artists painted a lion's heart, with students as the heart of the school. The mural at 34-20 94th Street is a heartbeat. When you look at it, you are hearing the lionhearts roar.

Another mural at IS 117 was called "The Day it All Changed," created by Abby Walsh. The historical context is about March 13, 2020, the day schools closed for the pandemic. The students painted that moment: the announcement, the disbelief, the goodbye to friends not knowing when they would return. The mural at 1865 Morris Avenue is a freeze frame. When you look at it, you are reliving the day it all changed.

PS 280Q got another mural in 2021 called "The Garden," created by Abby Walsh and Fermin Mendoza. The historical context is about growth and renewal after the pandemic. The artists painted a garden where flowers represented the students, blooming again after a long winter. The mural at 34-20 94th Street is a spring. When you look at it, you are watching the garden grow.

Horizon Juvenile Detention Center in Melrose, Bronx, got a mural in 2021 called "Headspace," created by Abby Walsh and Stephen Uhey. The historical context is about the mental health of incarcerated youth. The artists painted the inside of a head, showing thoughts, feelings, and memories. The mural at 360 E 145th Street is a brain scan. When you look at it, you are entering their headspace.

column10: Father Capodanno Blvd & Hunter Ave, Staten Island, NY 10305
column13: NYC Homecoming Week came to Staten Island in 2021, and a mural was created at Midland Beach by artists ADM and Cramcept. The historical context is about the city reopening after the pandemic. The artists painted a celebration: fireworks, dancing, and the Staten Island Ferry. The mural at Father Capodanno Boulevard and Hunter Avenue is a party. When you look at it, you are celebrating homecoming.

column10: Father Capodanno Blvd & Hunter Ave, Staten Island, NY 10305
column13: Another Homecoming Week mural at Midland Beach was called "NYC Strong," created by AIR3 and LASK. The historical context is about the resilience of New Yorkers. The artists painted the NYC skyline with a superhero cape, the words "NYC Strong" in bold letters. The mural at the same location is a flex. When you look at it, you are seeing New York strong.

NY Chinese Alliance Church on the Bowery got a mural in 2021 called "Spread Love, Stop Asian Hate," created by Bianca Romero. The historical context is about the rise in anti-Asian hate crimes during the pandemic. The artists painted hearts, flowers, and the words "Spread Love, Stop Asian Hate" in English and Chinese. The mural at 70-74 Mulberry Street is a protest. When you look at it, you are standing with the Asian community.

column1: NYC Homecoming Week: Brooklyn Keeps on Takin' It
column13: NYC Homecoming Week in Brooklyn got a mural at the Brooklyn Army Terminal called "Brooklyn Keeps on Takin' It," created by CHINO BYI and RIBS GAK. The historical context is about Brooklyn's unbreakable spirit. The artists painted the Brooklyn Bridge, the skyline, and the words "Brooklyn Keeps on Takin' It." The mural at 140 58th Street is a anthem. When you look at it, you are hearing Brooklyn's voice.

column1: South Bronx Community Charter High School: Design your Future
column2: South Bronx Community Charter High School
column13: South Bronx Community Charter High School in Morrisania got a mural in 2021 called "Design Your Future," created by Colleen Kong-Savage and Fermin Mendoza. The historical context is about the power of design thinking. The artists painted students drawing blueprints, building models, and creating prototypes. The mural at 925 Kelly Street is a workshop. When you look at it, you are designing your future.

column6: Cori Santana, Marissa Molina, Rob Ayala
column13: Union Settlement in East Harlem got a mural in 2021 called "Dreams for NYC," created by Cori Santana, Marissa Molina, and Rob Ayala. The historical context is about the organization's 125 years of serving the community. The artists painted the dreams of East Harlem residents, past and present. The mural at 237 E 104th Street is a vision board. When you look at it, you are seeing dreams for NYC.

column1: NYC Homecoming Week: Brooklyn Ready or Not
column6: Jenna Morello, Michela Muserra, CHINO-BYI, Miki-Mu, RIBS-GAK
column13: Another Homecoming Week mural at the Brooklyn Army Terminal was called "Brooklyn Ready or Not," created by Jenna Morello, Michela Muserra, CHINO-BYI, Miki-Mu, and RIBS-GAK. The historical context is about Brooklyn's confidence. The artists painted a Brooklyn player crossing over, with the words "Ready or Not." The mural at 140 58th Street is a crossover. When you look at it, you are seeing Brooklyn come.

Smile Juice Shop in East Harlem got a mural in 2021 created by Jon Souza. The historical context is about the juice shop's mission to bring happiness to the neighborhood. Souza painted a giant smile, with fruits and vegetables shooting out like juice. The mural at 225 E 104th Street is a grin. When you look at it, you are smiling.

Downtown Natural Market in Little Caribbean got a mural in 2021 called "Food for Thought," created by Jon Souza, TooFly, and Colleen Kong-Savage. The historical context is about the connection between food and learning. The artists painted a brain made of fruits and vegetables, with the words "Food for Thought." The mural at 888 Flatbush Avenue is a meal. When you look at it, you are eating food for thought.

column10: 1601 Morning Breeze Ln, National City, CA 91950
column13: Concrete & Canvas in National City, California, got a mural in 2021 called "Wonder Women," created by Julio Olvera. The historical context is about celebrating women in the community. Olvera painted portraits of local women who are wonder women in their own right: mothers, teachers, nurses, and activists. The mural at 1601 Morning Breeze Lane is a tribute. When you look at it, you are seeing wonder women.

column2: P.S. 89Q The Jose Peralta School of Dreamers
column13: P.S. 89Q The Jose Peralta School of Dreamers in Elmhurst got a mural in 2021 called "Tree of Life," created by Kristen Hubbard, @unlazyart, Colleen Kong-Savage, and @dyedinred. column1: Coney Island Gospel Assembly: Faith, Hope, and Love
column13: Coney Island Gospel Assembly got a mural in 2022 called "Faith, Hope, and Love," created by Andrea Amanda, Lase, Nicer, and Bio. The mural at 2828 Neptune Avenue is a sermon. When you look at it, you are hearing "Faith, hope, and love remain. And the greatest of these is love."

2022 was a big year for the young people at BronxConnect RTG North in West Farms, because that was the year a brand new music studio finally opened its doors. To celebrate, lead artist Ashley "Awesum" Crawford painted "Good Music" right inside the community center. Her mural features a giant microphone and a boy surfing across piano keys, alongside a line from Bob Marley: "One good thing about music, when it hits you, you feel no pain." For a neighborhood where gun violence had stolen too many young lives, those words were more than decoration. They were medicine. The mural became a promise that every kid walking through the doors could find healing on a beat or a melody, turning pain into something powerful.

column1: IS 117/The Young Women's Leadership School: Rich Tapestry
column6: Ashley Crawford, Kristy McCarthy, Joshua Gabriel, Marissa Molina, Vickie, Sydney Tirado
column13: Picture the hallways of IS 117 in Mount Hope, the Bronx, in 2022. That year, artists Ashley Crawford and Kristy McCarthy led art lessons with more than a hundred students from the middle school and The Young Women's Leadership School. The principals wanted a mural that celebrated inclusion, diversity, and respect, because their students came from every walk of life. The young artists created pieces focused on the beauty of varied perspectives, with an emphasis on honoring the African, Islamic, and LGBTQ+ communities. The finished work is called "Rich Tapestry," a title pulled from a Maya Angelou quote featured right in the design: "We all should know that diversity makes for a rich tapestry, and we must understand that all the threads of the tapestry are equal in value no matter what their color." It is a reminder that every voice, every story, every identity is a thread worth treasuring.
