column13: In 2022, the street artist Michela "Miki Mu" Muserra unveiled a mural titled "Rat & Pigeon Chillin' in Miami" during Art Basel Miami Beach. This piece marked her first mural in Miami for the event and was sponsored by organizations including Thrive Collective and Bed Stuy Walls

Think of an office hallway in a Manhattan building in 2022. The pandemic had just forced everyone to stay home for two years, and NYU's Opportunity Project, a program that supports first generation, low income New York State students, knew its staff needed more than just a desk. They needed a reminder that they were part of something bigger. So they reached out to Thrive Collective and Brooklyn based artist Michela Muserra, an Italian born illustrator who has called New York home since 2003. The result was "We are OP," a mural designed not just to beautify the space but to spark conversation and rebuild the feeling of belonging that the pandemic had taken away. Every student who steps into that office now sees a splash of color and a quietly powerful message: you belong here, and you are not alone.

This was a cncrete fortress that once shipped supplies for two world wars. Now, the NYC Economic Development Corporation has transformed it into a hub for modern industry and small businesses. PS 132 in Washington Heights got a mural in 2023 called "Juan Pablo Duarte," created by Toofly and Kenneth Tooley. The historical context is about Dominican heritage. Juan Pablo Duarte is the father of Dominican independence. The artists painted his portrait alongside Dominican flags, flowers, and the faces of students. The mural at 201 East 184th Street is a history lesson. When you look at it, you are learning that you come from heroes.

column6: Toofly, Kenneth Tooley, Loreto, Mirari Hernandez
column13: PS 205K in Bensonhurst, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2023 called "All are Welcome," created by Toofly, Kenneth Tooley, Loreto, and Mirari Hernandez. The historical context is about inclusion. The artists painted the phrase in multiple languages, alongside open doors and smiling faces from every background. The mural at 85-28 Britton Avenue in Elmhurst is a welcome mat. When you look at it, you are being invited in. No matter who you are. All are welcome.

column1: P.S. 89Q The Jose Peralta School of Dreamers: Our Dreams
column2: P.S. 89Q The Jose Peralta School of Dreamers
column13: P.S. 89Q The Jose Peralta School of Dreamers in Elmhurst, Queens, got a mural in 2023 called "Our Dreams," created by Toofly, May Bukowski, and Chris. The historical context is about the school's name. Jose Peralta was a state senator who fought for Dreamers, undocumented immigrants brought to the US as children. The artists painted students' dreams, college, careers, and families, floating above their heads like clouds. The mural at 101 Maujer Street in Brooklyn is a wish list. When you look at it, you are seeing that Dreamers deserve to dream too.

column6: Vanesa Álvarez Díaz, Arantxa X. Rodríguez, Andrea Amanda, Danny Diodato
column13: PS 18 in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2023 called "We, the Power 2," created by Vanesa Álvarez Díaz, Arantxa X. Rodríguez, Andrea Amanda, and Danny Diodato. The historical context is about the sequel. We, the Power 1 was so successful that the school asked for a second. The artists painted students organizing, protesting, and voting. The mural at 101 Maujer Street is a civics lesson. When you look at it, you are learning that you have power. Use it.

column1: PS 18 Edward Bush: The Magic Wall
column6: Vanesa Álvarez Díaz, Loreto Hart, Sydney Tirado, Kenneth Tooley
column13: PS 18 Edward Bush got another mural in 2023 called "The Magic Wall," created by Vanesa Álvarez Díaz, Loreto Hart, Sydney Tirado, and Kenneth Tooley. The historical context is about imagination. A blank wall is boring. A painted wall is magic. The artists painted wizards, dragons, and enchanted forests. The mural at 2252 Ryer Avenue in the Bronx is a spell. When you look at it, you are being transported to another world.

Another PS 9X lunchroom mural was created by Vince Ballantine and Victoria DeJesus in 2023. The historical context is about fuel. Food is fuel for your body and brain. Ballantine painted engines, batteries, and power bars alongside images of healthy food. The mural at 1250 Jerome Avenue is a gas station. When you look at it, you are filling up your tank.

column6: Will DeNatale, Emily Gooden, Marissa Molina, Savannah Zambrano, May Bukowski
column13: PS 279X Captain Manuel Rivera, Jr. in Fordham Heights got two murals in 2023 both called "Fruitful," created by Will DeNatale, Emily Gooden, Marissa Molina, Savannah Zambrano, and May Bukowski. The first focused on academic fruit, like good grades and graduation. The murals at 1250 Jerome Avenue are an orchard. When you look at them, you are seeing that hard work bears fruit.

column6: Will DeNatale, Emily Gooden, Marissa Molina, Savannah Zambrano, May Bukowski
column13: The second "Fruitful" mural focused on character fruit, like kindness and honesty. The mural at 232 E 184th Street is a reminder that being good also bears fruit.

column1: PS 33: To Learn is to Grow
column6: Will DeNatale, Lola Lovenotes, Emily Gooden, Marissa Molina, Pips
column13: PS 33 in Fordham Heights, Bronx, got a mural in 2023 called "To Learn is to Grow," created by Will DeNatale, Lola Lovenotes, Emily Gooden, Marissa Molina, and Pips. The historical context is about the purpose of school. Learning is not about filling a bucket. It is about growing a garden. The artists painted seeds becoming plants, and plants becoming trees, with books as water and teachers as sun. The mural at 100 Tompkins Avenue on Staten Island is a metaphor. When you look at it, you are seeing that every day you learn, you grow.

column1: Peace in the Park: Stop the Violence Staten Island
column13: Another Peace in the Park mural on Staten Island was created by artist Will Power in 2023. The historical context is about the power of one person to stop violence. Will Power painted a single figure standing between two fighters, arms outstretched. The mural at 35 Hill Street is an intervention. When you look at it, you are being asked to be that person. The one who steps in.

column1: CHARAS/El Bohio Community Center: El Bohio Murals
column13: CHARAS/El Bohio Community Center on the Lower East Side got a series of murals in 2023 called "El Bohio Murals," created by Will Power and Al Diaz, who was Jean Michel Basquiat's partner in the SAMO graffiti duo. The historical context is about the building itself. The abandoned school at 605 East 9th Street has been a community hub for decades. The artists painted tributes to the neighborhood's Puerto Rican, Dominican, and activist history. The murals are an archive. When you look at them, you are reading the history of Loisaida.

column13: The Hip Hop 50th Birthday Jam at Mill Pond Park in the Bronx also got a mural in 2023 about the future of hip hop, created by Will Power, BG 183, Bio, Nicer, Lady Pink, Queen Andrea, Michela Muserra, and May Bukowski. The historical context is about what comes next. Hip hop is 50 years old, but it is not done. The artists painted children holding microphones, spraying graffiti, and dancing. The mural at East 149th Street and Exterior Street is a prophecy. When you look at it, you are seeing that the future of hip hop is in good hands. The next 50 years start now.

PS 94X in Norwood, Bronx, got a mural in 2024 called "Pride," created by artist Andre Trenier. The historical context is about the school's lion mascot and core values: Respect, Ownership, Awareness, Responsibility. Trenier painted a family of lions relaxed and enjoying their home, a visual metaphor for the pride students should feel in their school and themselves. The mural at 1920 Benedict Avenue is a daily reminder that pride is not arrogance. Pride is knowing who you are and where you belong.

PS/MS 7M in East Harlem, Manhattan, got a mural in 2024 called "We Rise Together," created by artist Andre Trenier. East Harlem has faced challenges, but the community has always risen together. Trenier painted hands lifting each other, students climbing stairs side by side, and a sun rising over the neighborhood. The mural at 210 East 117th Street is a promise that no one rises alone.

column2: Lower Manhattan Academy of Arts High School

column13: Lower Manhattan Arts Academy, known as LOMA, on the Lower East Side got a mural in 2024 called "LOMA Energy," created by Ashley Crawford with Sydney Tirado, Pelumi Ayeni, Joshua Gabriel, Andrea Amanda, and Colleen Kong Savage. LOMA is an arts high school, and energy is everything. The artists painted vibrant waves of color, dancing figures, and musical notes pulsing through the hallways. The mural at 10 Rivington Street is a battery recharge of young artists at work.

column1: Hyde Leadership Charter School: Hyde Heroes on the Road to Success
column6: Ashley Crawford, Sydney Tirado, Andrea Amanda, Kenneth Tooley, Pelumi Ayeni, Yukiko Izumi, Will DeNatale, Peter Yi
column13: Hyde Leadership Charter School in East New York, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2024 called "Hyde Heroes on the Road to Success," created by a large team of eight artists. The school's leadership model teaches that every student can be a hero. The artists painted students as superheroes on a journey, facing obstacles and growing stronger. The mural at 664 Vermont Street is a comic book in paint showing that heroes are made on the road to success.

column1: PS 92 x Brooklyn Nets: The Brooklyn Way
column13: PS 92 in Flatbush, Brooklyn, partnered with the Brooklyn Nets in 2024 for a mural called "The Brooklyn Way," created by Ashley Crawford and Wale Ayeni. The Brooklyn Way means grit, resilience, and community. The artists painted basketball players alongside students, showing that the same skills that win games also win at life. The mural at 5900 Glenwood Road is a crossover dribble between sports and education.

column6: Ashley Crawford, Wale Ayeni, Kenneth Tooley, Marissa Molina, Pelumi Ayeni
column13: Queens Preparatory Academy in Rochdale, Queens, got a mural in 2024 called "The Most Powerful Weapon," created by Ashley Crawford, Wale Ayeni, Kenneth Tooley, Marissa Molina, and Pelumi Ayeni. The title comes from a famous quote: "The most powerful weapon on earth is the human soul on fire." The artists painted students with flames in their hearts, charging forward into their futures. The mural at 143-10 Springfield Boulevard is a battle cry of young people armed with passion.

NYCHA Jacob Riis in the East Village, Manhattan, got a mural in 2024 called "Choose Joy," created by BG183, Bio, and Nicer. Life in public housing can be hard, but joy is a choice. The artists painted bright colors, smiling faces, and the word JOY in large letters. The mural at 600 East 6th Street is a daily decision to choose joy, even on the hardest days.

NYCHA Jacob Riis in the East Village, Manhattan, got a second mural in 2024 called "Create Memories," created by BG183, Bio, and Nicer. The artists painted families laughing, children playing, and neighbors gathering to remind residents that every day is a chance to create a memory. The mural at 600 East 6th Street is a photo album urging you not to waste a single day.

The Queens HeART Beat Festival in South Jamaica got a mural in 2024 called "Peace & Love" focused on Peace, created by Chey Nelson and Colleen Kong Savage. The artists painted doves, olive branches, and calm faces to express what every community wants most. The mural at 177-01 Baisley Boulevard is a wish for peace.

The Queens HeART Beat Festival in South Jamaica got a second mural in 2024 also called "Peace & Love" but focused on Love, created by Chey Nelson and Colleen Kong Savage. The artists painted hearts, hugs, and the word LOVE in bright colors. The mural at 177-01 Baisley Boulevard is a feeling reminding you that love is always the answer.

column6: Chey Nelson, Miri Banana, Collen Kong Savage
column13: PS 171Q in Astoria, Queens, got a mural in 2024 called "Model for our Future," created by Chey Nelson, Miri Banana, and Collen Kong Savage. Every student is a model for someone. The artists painted students as role models helping others, studying hard, and dreaming big. The mural at 14-14 29th Avenue is a fashion show of character showing that the future looks bright.

column13: Aiken Street Playground in Baltimore, Maryland, got a mural in 2024 called "Aiken Street Joy," created by Christian Penn. Playgrounds should be joyful. Penn painted children swinging, sliding, and laughing in bright colors. The mural at Aiken Street and East Federal Street is a laugh track where you can almost hear the children screaming with delight.

column2: SOME (So Others Might Eat) Community Center
column13: SOME (So Others Might Eat) community center in Washington D.C. got a mural in 2024 called "Community," created by Christian Penn. SOME provides food, housing, and care to those in need. Penn painted hands reaching out, meals being shared, and neighbors helping neighbors. The mural at 45 Q Street NE is a mission statement of what community really means.

Kings Plaza Mall in Mill Basin, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2024 created by Cramcept that simply says "Brooklyn" in bold, colorful letters. Public art in commercial spaces is rare, but this mural declares identity loud and clear. The mural at 5100 Kings Plaza is a declaration that Brooklyn pride cannot be contained, not even in a mall.

column10: 1363 Edward L Grant Hwy, Bronx, NY 10452
column13: The Bronx High School for Visual Arts (BHSVA) got a mural in 2024 called "PROSPER Basketball Court," created by legendary graffiti artists Crash and Daze. The artists painted the word PROSPER on the basketball court surrounded by vibrant colors and patterns. The court at 1363 Edward L Grant Highway is both a gallery and a gym, showing that art belongs everywhere, even where sneakers squeak.

column1: Atlantic Ave BID: The Heart of Brooklyn
column13: Atlantic Avenue BID in Boerum Hill, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2024 called "The Heart of Brooklyn," created by Danielle Mastrion at the Atlantic Grill & Deli. Atlantic Avenue is full of family owned shops and restaurants. Mastrion painted a giant anatomical heart whose chambers were filled with local landmarks. The mural at 293 Atlantic Avenue is a love letter to the heartbeat of Brooklyn.

column13: The seventh PS 60 mural was "NYC," a skyline of the city's most famous buildings including the Statue of Liberty, the Empire State Building, and the Brooklyn Bridge. The mural at 55 Merrill Avenue is a postcard reminding you why you love New York.

Peace in the Park, Vol 2 at PS 78 on Staten Island got a mural in 2024 called "Unity," created by Dylan Giangrande. The artists painted figures of all ages, races, and abilities holding hands in a circle. The mural at 1821 S 35th Street in San Diego is a message that unity is possible with work.

Another Peace in the Park, Vol 2 mural at PS 78 on Staten Island was created by Jodi Dareal, who painted a peaceful garden with children reading, playing, and resting. The mural at 80 Maple Parkway is a sanctuary where you can find peace.

PS 44 on Staten Island got a Healthy Living Series of three murals in 2024 created by Jodi Dareal. The first was "Healthy Living," featuring fruits, vegetables, exercise, and sleep. The mural at 80 Maple Parkway is a doctor's prescription to take care of your body.

column13: The second PS 44 mural was "Watch Me Soar," featuring children flying like birds with capes and confident smiles. The mural at 80 Maple Parkway is a pep talk telling you to spread your wings.

The second PS 20 mural was "Meditation," featuring a student sitting cross legged, eyes closed, breathing deeply. The mural at 60 Merrill Avenue is a yoga class teaching you to breathe.
The third PS 20 mural was "Serenity," with soft colors, gentle waves, and quiet animals. The mural at 60 Merrill Avenue is a lullaby that makes you feel sleepy.

column13: Leadership & Public Service High School in the Financial District, Manhattan, got a mural in 2024 called "Welcome," created by Kristy McCarthy and Pelumi Ayeni. column13: FDR High School in Mapleton, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2024 called "The Foundations of Science," created by Kristy McCarthy and Yukiko Izumi with students Daniel and Alexa. PS 78 on Staten Island got a mural in 2024 called "We Care," created by Lina Montoya and Mona Oman. The artists painted children helping each other, sharing toys, and wiping tears. The mural at 80 Maple Parkway is a lesson that caring is a verb. Do it.

PS 12X Lewis and Clark School in Westchester Square, Bronx, got a mural in 2024 called "Grow Forever," created by Lola Lovenotes and Gloria Zapata. column13: John Dewey High School in Gravesend, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2024 called "The John Dewey Student Is ..." created by Marissa Molina and Christine DiPasquale. Students answered with words like "artist," "friend," "dreamer," and "leader." The mural at 730 E 12th Street is a collection of self portraits, each one a declaration of identity.

column1: Gershwin Campus x Brooklyn Nets: The Brooklyn Way
column13: The Gershwin Campus in East New York, Brooklyn, partnered with the Brooklyn Nets in 2024 to create "The Brooklyn Way," a mural by May Bukowski. The Nets' motto is about grit, resilience, and community. Bukowski painted basketball imagery alongside scenes of students working together, studying together, and celebrating together. The mural at 5700 Avenue H is a sports arena and a classroom combined, showing that the same qualities of a great athlete also make a great student.

column1: Park East High School: Rhythms of 105
column13: Park East High School in El Barrio, Manhattan, received a mural in 2024 called "Rhythms of 105," created by May Bukowski. East 105th Street has its own heartbeat, its own sounds, its own rhythm. Bukowski painted musical notes, dancers, and the flow of daily life. The mural at 230 E 105th Street is a love letter to a school and a neighborhood where you can almost hear the rhythm of 105.

column1: Park East High School: Rhythms of 105
column13: The second Park East High School mural was also called "Rhythms of 105," this one quieter, focusing on moments between classes, a student reading alone, a teacher grading papers, a janitor sweeping the floor. The mural at 230 E 105th Street is the quiet verse of the same song.

Star Academy PS 63 on the Lower East Side got a mural in 2024 called "Vibrations of LES," created by May Bukowski. The Lower East Side vibrates with history, from tenement immigrants to punk rock to today's artists and dreamers. Bukowski painted that vibration as colorful waves pulsing through the streets and into the school. The mural at 121 E 3rd Street is a seismograph of the neighborhood, showing the invisible energy of a place that has always been a home for outsiders.

Peace in the Park, Vol 2 came to PS 78 on Staten Island in 2024, created by Michela "Miki Mu" Muserra. The original Peace in the Park mural was so beloved that the community asked for a sequel. Miki Mu painted scenes of children playing, families picnicking, and neighbors waving to each other. The mural at 80 Maple Parkway is a sequel that outdoes the original, showing that peace is not a one time thing but a series, volume after volume, year after year.

column1: Amazin' Mets Foundation x CS 111Q: So Amazin'
column13: The Amazin' Mets Foundation partnered with CS 111 in Queensbridge for a mural called "So Amazin'" in 2024, created by Michela Muserra and Chey Nelson. Queensbridge is the largest public housing complex in North America, and it has produced legends in music, sports, and art. The artists painted Mets colors, baseball imagery, and portraits of local heroes. The mural at 31-51 21st Street in Long Island City is a home run, showing a community that loves its team and loves itself.

The Queens HeART Beat Festival in South Jamaica got a mural in 2024 called "Play," created by Michela Muserra. In a neighborhood where children often grow up too fast, Play is a reminder of what they deserve. Muserra painted hopscotch, jump rope, and kids running through sprinklers. The mural at 177-01 Baisley Boulevard is a playground in paint, teaching that play is not a waste of time but how children learn, grow, and heal.

PS 197K in Midwood, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2024 called "Path of Learning," created by Michela Muserra. Learning is not a destination. It is a path. Muserra painted a winding road with signposts marking different subjects: math, reading, science, art, and friendship. The mural at 3400 Avenue M is a map showing that every student is on their own path, but all paths lead somewhere important. Keep walking.

P.S. 89Q in Elmhurst, Queens, got a mural in 2024 called "Food Party," created by Michela Muserra and Christopher Gonzalez. Elmhurst is one of the most diverse neighborhoods in the world, famous for its restaurants with cuisine from every continent. The artists painted a feast featuring dishes from the students' own cultures: dumplings, empanadas, samosas, and tacos all on one table. The mural at 54-23 Justice Avenue is a potluck where food is culture, memory, and love.

column1: BedStuy Walls: Third Annual Mural Festival
column13: BedStuy Walls hosted its third annual mural festival in 2024 at 677 Lexington Avenue, created by Michela Muserra and Frankie Velez. Bed Stuy Walls has become a beloved annual event, turning the neighborhood into an outdoor gallery. The artists painted a vibrant, community centered piece that reflected the spirit of Bedford Stuyvesant. The mural is a family reunion showing that some traditions get better every year.

column1: 12C Outdoor Murals: Despues de la Lluvia
column6: Michela Muserra, Savannah Zambrano, Danielle Mastrion
column13: The 12C Outdoor Gallery in Loisaida, Manhattan, got a mural in 2024 called "Despues de la Lluvia" (After the Rain), created by Michela Muserra, Savannah Zambrano, and Danielle Mastrion. The Lower East Side has seen its share of storms, both literal and figurative. The artists painted a rainbow emerging from dark clouds, flowers blooming in wet soil, and children jumping in puddles. The mural at 730 E 12th Street is a promise that the rain always stops and the sun always returns.

PS 74 on Staten Island got a series of affirmation murals in 2024 created by Mona Oman. What you say to yourself matters. Oman painted emojis, positive words, and bright colors across the school. The murals at 175 Warner Avenue are a daily dose of kindness, reminding you to be gentle with yourself. You are enough. You are loved. You matter.

column1: BedStuy NeON: The Rhythm of Bed Stuy
column13: The NeON Arts Festival in Bed Stuy, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2024 called "The Rhythm of Bed Stuy," created by Nico Collazo with Marissa Molina and Wale Ayeni. Bed Stuy has a rhythm all its own, from the boom of stereos to the chatter on stoops to the clap of church hands. The artists painted that rhythm as colorful sound waves, dancing figures, and musical notes. The mural at 10 E 135th Street is a song you can see. Listen closely.

column1: Frank McCourt HS: Inspire Growth Daily
column13: Frank McCourt High School on the Upper West Side got a mural in 2024 called "Inspire Growth Daily," created by Nico Collazo. Every day, students come to school to grow, not just academically but as people. Collazo painted images of seeds becoming trees, children becoming adults, and dreams becoming reality. The mural at 161 E 161st Street in the Bronx is a daily mission statement asking, "Did you grow today? Did you inspire someone else to grow?"

The Bronx NeON festival at 161 Studio in Melrose got a mural in 2024 created by Nico Collazo and Marissa Molina. 161 Studio is a community arts space where young people can create freely. The artists painted a colorful, abstract celebration of that freedom. The mural at 2820 W 33rd Street in Brooklyn is a thank you note to the studio, showing that art saves lives and gave these young people a place to belong.

column1: PS 188 x Brooklyn Nets x NYCHA Gravesend: The Brooklyn Way
column13: PS 188 in Coney Island partnered with the Brooklyn Nets and NYCHA Gravesend in 2024 for a mural called "The Brooklyn Way," created by Peach Tao and Chris Gonzalez. NYCHA residents often go unseen, but this mural put them in the spotlight. The artists painted basketball players, families, and the iconic Brooklyn Bridge. The mural at 87 Bay 49th Street is a slam dunk showing that the Brooklyn Way is not just for celebrities. It is for everyone.

column2: P.S 212 The Lady Deborah Moody School
column13: P.S. 212 The Lady Deborah Moody School in Gravesend, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2024 called "P.S 212 Has the Best Koalities," created by Pelumi Ayeni. Koalities sounds like qualities, and the koala is the school mascot. Ayeni painted koalas demonstrating positive character traits: kindness, honesty, respect, and perseverance. The mural at 2360 Benson Avenue is a spelling lesson and a character lesson in one, showing that the best qualities are not about being smart or fast but about being good.

P.S. 101 The Verrazano in Gravesend, Brooklyn, got a Workspace Series of six murals in 2024 created by Pelumi Ayeni and Marissa Molina. The first was "Custodian Engineer," honoring invisible work. The artists painted a custodian as a superhero with mop as cape and broom as staff. The mural at 2360 Benson Avenue is a thank you for every job that is noble when done with care.

column1: P.S. 101: Workspace Series / Journey of Technology
column13: The second P.S. 101 mural was "Journey of Technology," showing a timeline from typewriters to laptops with students at every stage. The mural at 2360 Benson Avenue is a history lesson that technology is not magic but a journey, and these students are the latest travelers.

The third P.S. 101 mural was "Main Office," a welcoming scene for the front desk with smiling faces, helpful hands, and the words "How can I help you?" The mural at 2360 Benson Avenue is a greeting that makes sure the main office feels like home.

The fourth P.S. 101 mural was "Nurse's Office," a calming scene with bandages, teddy bears, and a thermometer that reads "You'll be okay." The mural at 2360 Benson Avenue is a comfort teaching that getting hurt is part of life, but so is getting better.

column1: P.S. 101: Workspace Series / Showcasing the World
column13: The fifth P.S. 101 mural was "Showcasing the World," a map of the globe with flags from every country the students come from, plus landmarks, foods, and traditional clothing. The mural at 2360 Benson Avenue is a passport showing that the world is not far away; the world is in this school.

The sixth P.S. 101 mural was "Tech Deck," a celebration of the school's computer lab with keyboards, mice, screens, students coding, and creating. The mural at 2360 Benson Avenue is a startup office showing that technology is not just for playing games but for building the future.

IS 117X in Mount Hope, Bronx, got a mural in 2024 called "Embrace," created by Pips. The world is hard. School is hard. But embrace can make it easier. Pips painted arms open wide, hugging students of all backgrounds. The mural at 1865 Morris Avenue is a warm embrace in paint form, holding you not physically but emotionally.

column1: PS 50Q: The Beginning of PS 50 Stars
column6: Plushie, Chey Nelson, Colleen Kong Savage, Pips
column13: PS 50Q in Jamaica, Queens, got a mural in 2024 called "The Beginning of PS 50 Stars," created by Plushie, Chey Nelson, Colleen Kong Savage, and Pips. Every star has a beginning. The artists painted students as young stars, some still in cocoons, others already glowing. The mural at 146-11 101st Avenue is an origin story showing that greatness does not happen overnight. It starts small. It starts here.

column1: Fannie Lou Hamer Middle School Values
column13: Fannie Lou Hamer Middle School in Crotona Park, Bronx, got three murals in 2024 created by Queen Andrea and Gloria Zapata. The first was "Lead with Love." Fannie Lou Hamer was a civil rights icon who led with love in the face of hatred. The artists painted her famous words alongside images of young leaders. The mural at 1001 Jennings Street is a history lesson that love is not weak but the most powerful force for change.

column1: Fannie Lou Hamer Middle School Values
column13: The second Fannie Lou Hamer mural was "Chase Your Dreams," with students running after their dreams that looked like diplomas, musical instruments, and sports trophies. The mural at 1001 Jennings Street is a race track telling you to run, not walk. Your dreams are waiting.

column1: Fannie Lou Hamer Middle School Values
column13: The third Fannie Lou Hamer mural was "You Matter," the simplest and most important message of all. The artists painted the words in bold letters surrounded by mirrors so students could see themselves. The mural at 1001 Jennings Street is a reflection where you see your own face and read the words "You Matter." That is the whole lesson.

PS 56Q in Richmond Hill, Queens, got a mural in 2024 called "GRIT Basketball Court," created by Queen Andrea and Shiro. The court was old and cracked, but the students kept playing. The artists painted the word GRIT in large letters along with images of players diving for loose balls and taking charges. The mural on the court at 86-10 114th Street is a coach's speech teaching that talent is not enough. You need grit. Heart. Determination.

Another "Peace in the Park, Vol 2" mural at PS 78 on Staten Island was created by Riiisa Boogie in 2024. Miki Mu painted one version; Riiisa Boogie painted another. This one focused on togetherness, with figures of all ages holding hands in a circle. The mural at 100 Tompkins Avenue is a community hug showing that peace takes many forms, but it always includes connection.

column1: Cedar Hill High School: Cedar Hill CHARGE!
column13: Cedar Hill High School in Cedar Hill, Texas, got a mural in 2024 called "Cedar Hill CHARGE!" created by Sam Wisneski and Ray Albarez. The Chargers are the school's mascot. The artists painted a massive charging horse with students on its back. The mural at 1 Longhorn Boulevard is a pep rally where you can hear the crowd roar. CHARGE!

DeSoto High School in DeSoto, Texas, got a mural in 2024 called "Ready to Soar," also created by Sam Wisneski and Ray Albarez. Every senior is ready to leave the nest and soar. The artists painted eagles taking flight with students holding diplomas and waving goodbye. The mural at 600 Eagle Drive is a commencement speech where you can hear "Pomp and Circumstance." Ready to soar? Then fly.

column6: Savannah Zambrano, Danielle Mastrion, Michela Muserra
column10: E 12th St & Ave C, New York, NY 10009
column13: The 12C Outdoor Gallery in Loisaida got another mural in 2024 called "Basquiat's Loisaida," created by Savannah Zambrano, Danielle Mastrion, and Michela Muserra. Jean Michel Basquiat grew up in Loisaida, and his graffiti art changed the world. The artists painted a tribute to Basquiat's style with crowns, skulls, and scribbled words. The mural at E 12th St & Ave C is a museum showing that greatness can come from anywhere, even from this corner.

column1: Amazin' Mets Foundation x PS 14Q: So Amazin'
column13: The Amazin' Mets Foundation partnered with PS 14 in Corona, Queens, for a mural called "So Amazin'" in 2024, created by Toofly. Toofly grew up in Corona and attended PS 14 as a child. Now she returned to paint a mural for her old school. The mural was painted at Citi Field during Hispanic Heritage Night then donated to PS 14. The mural at 107-01 Otis Avenue is a homecoming showing that you can go home again, and when you do, you can bring a paintbrush.

column6: Toofly, Ayana Ayo, Lola Lovenotes, Tierra
column13: MS 484K in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2024 called "Beautiful," created by Toofly, Ayana Ayo, Lola Lovenotes, and Tierra. In a world that tells young people, especially young Black and Brown people, that they are not enough, this mural shouts the opposite. The artists painted the words "I Am Beautiful. We Are Beautiful" across the wall at 430 Howard Avenue, alongside Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s words "I have a dream!" The mural is a daily reminder that you are beautiful not because of what you achieve but because you exist.

PS 354Q in Jamaica, Queens, got a mural in 2024 called "Let's Build!" created by Toofly and Joshua Gabriel. The artists asked students what they wanted to build. The answers became the mural: towers of blocks, bridges made of books, and skylines built from dreams. The mural at 126-10 Bedell Street is an invitation to every child to be a builder of careers, families, and communities.

PS 132M in Washington Heights, Manhattan, got a mural in 2024 called "Breathe," created by Toofly, Joshua Gabriel, and Loretoh Art. Washington Heights is a busy, fast paced neighborhood where students carry heavy burdens. The artists painted deep breaths as colorful waves, calm faces, and quiet moments of rest. The mural at 185 Wadsworth Avenue is a pause button reminding you to stop, inhale, and exhale. That simple act can change everything.

column6: Tsvetana Dondero, Krystal Romero Granell, Gabriel Abast
column10: Calle Maria Casado A18, Canóvanas, PR 00729
column13: In Canóvanas, Puerto Rico, Academia Bautista Sotera Sanchez received a mural in 2024 called "Una Nueva Generación de Amabilidad" (A New Generation of Kindness), created by Tsvetana Dondero, Krystal Romero Granell, and Gabriel Abast. Puerto Rico was still healing from Hurricane Maria and the earthquakes. The students painted kindness as the way forward, not revenge or anger. The mural at Calle Maria Casado A18 is a promise that the next generation will be different. They will be kind.

column2: Colegio Católico Nuestra Señora del Pilar
column6: Tsvetana Dondero, Krystal Romero Granell, Gabriel Abast
column13: A second mural in Canóvanas, Puerto Rico, was called "Viajeros de Amabilidad" (Kindness Travelers), created at Colegio Católico Nuestra Señora del Pilar by the same team. Kindness does not stay in one place. It travels. The artists painted children carrying suitcases filled with love, compassion, and helpful hands. The mural at Calle Luis Hernaíz #3 shows kindness crossing borders, languages, and generations. Every student is a traveler who can carry kindness wherever they go.

column6: Vanesa Álvarez Díaz, Chris Gonzalez, Yukiko Izumi
column13: Corona Arts & Sciences Academy in North Corona, Queens, got a mural in 2024 called "Celebrate," created by Vanesa Álvarez Díaz, Chris Gonzalez, and Yukiko Izumi. Corona is one of the most diverse places on Earth, with families from Latin America, South Asia, and everywhere in between. The artists asked students what they wanted to celebrate. Their answers became the mural: quinceañeras, Eid, Diwali, Lunar New Year. The mural at 98-11 44th Avenue is a party in paint showing a community that chooses joy even when the world is heavy.

column6: Vanesa Álvarez Díaz, Plushie, Yukiko Izumi
column13: PS 18K in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, got two murals in 2024. The first was "Be a Star," created by Vanesa Álvarez Díaz, Plushie, and Yukiko Izumi. Williamsburg has changed dramatically, but the students at PS 18 have always been stars. The artists painted students as constellations, each one unique and brilliant. The mural at 101 Maujer Street is a reminder that you do not need to be famous to be a star. You just need to show up and be yourself. Shine.

column6: Vanesa Álvarez Díaz, Yukiko Izumi, Ashley Crawford
column13: The second mural at PS 18K was "Attendance Stars," created by Vanesa Álvarez Díaz, Yukiko Izumi, and Ashley Crawford. Every day a student comes to school, they are making a choice to learn, to grow, to be present. The artists painted stars next to attendance charts, celebrating the simple act of being there. The mural at 101 Maujer Street turns a routine statistic into a celebration that showing up is half the battle, and it is worth cheering for.

MS 61K in Prospect Lefferts Gardens, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2024 called "Futurism," created by Vince Ballantine. The future can be scary, but it can also be exciting. Ballantine painted images of flying cars, robot teachers, and students exploring new planets. The mural at 400 Empire Boulevard is a science fiction novel on a wall, showing a generation that is not afraid of tomorrow. They are ready for it.

column1: 0 Boone Avenue Walls 2024 Mural Festival (Bronx 2024) More Details
column13: Boone Avenue Walls in Mott Haven, Bronx, hosted a mural festival in 2024 featuring Wen Cod. Boone Avenue has become a destination for street art, turning an ordinary block into an outdoor gallery. Wen Cod painted a vibrant, abstract piece that brought color to a neighborhood that has seen too much grey. The mural at 1761 Boone Avenue is a celebration of public art as a community builder. One weekend, one wall, one neighborhood changed forever.

column6: Will DeNatale, Emily Gooden, Sydney Tirado
column13: PS 288K in Coney Island, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2024 called "Bloom Together," created by Will DeNatale, Emily Gooden, and Sydney Tirado. Coney Island was devastated by Hurricane Sandy in 2012, and the recovery has been slow, but flowers bloom even in sandy soil. The artists painted gardens growing, children helping each other, and a community rising together. The mural at 2727 Mermaid Avenue is a metaphor for Coney Island itself, showing resilience in full color. Bloom together.

PS 145K in Bushwick, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2024 called "Leadership through Engineering," created by Yazmeen Collazo and Ayana Ayo. PS 145 is a magnet school for leadership and engineering. The artists painted a system of gears in bright oranges, blues, and greens, greeting every visitor. The mural at 100 Tompkins Avenue is a visual mission statement showing that leadership and engineering are the same thing. Both require problem solving, teamwork, and building the future.

column1: RTG North: Brainiac Babies / Future Leaders
column13: In 2025, the Bronx neighborhood of West Farms saw something new and unexpected. Artist Ashley Crawford created "Brainiac Babies / Future Leaders" on Crotona Avenue, and the name alone makes you smile. West Farms has faced generations of neglect, but the children there are brilliant. Crawford painted babies wearing glasses, holding books, and looking like little professors. They are not cute for the sake of being cute. They are a declaration that intelligence starts young and that every child in this neighborhood is a future leader. When you stand before this mural at 2260 Crotona Avenue, you are seeing a community saying we will not wait until they are grown to believe in them. We believe in them right now, as babies, as scholars, as the future.

PS 371 Lillian Rashkis High School in Greenwood, Brooklyn, serves students who have taken nontraditional paths to their diplomas. In 2025, artists Ashley Crawford and Amber Smalls created "Pathways" to honor those journeys. Transfer schools like PS 371 are where students go when life got in the way, when they had to work, parent, or survive. Crawford and Smalls worked with students to paint images of roads, doors, and open skies. Each symbol said the same thing. Your path might look different, but it is still valid. The mural at 355 37th Street became a daily reminder that there is no single way to graduate. There is only your way.

column6: Ashley Crawford, Lola Lovenotes, May Bukowski, Ralph Demaio, Raissa Da Silva
column13: Marie Curie High School in the Bronx's Kingsbridge Heights has a motto. "One Community." In 2025, a team of five artists, Ashley Crawford, Lola Lovenotes, May Bukowski, Ralph Demaio, and Raissa Da Silva, helped students paint that motto on the walls. Kingsbridge Heights is a diverse pocket of the Bronx where Dominican, Irish, African American, and other families live side by side. The artists asked students what community meant to them. They drew shared meals, school hallways, and hands helping hands. The finished mural at 120 West 231st Street is a riot of color and faces, all different, all together. When you look at it, you are seeing the future of New York. A place where one community is not a slogan. It is a fact.

column6: Christian Bachez, Toofly, Lorena Barrezueta Carlo, Kadeem Phillip
column13: Dream Walls 3.0 came to PS/MS 34 on Manhattan's Lower East Side in 2025, nearly 20 years after the original Dream Walls project began. "The Classics" mural, created by Christian Bachez, Toofly, Lorena Barrezueta Carlo, and Kadeem Phillip, looked back at the artists and styles that started it all. In 2007, these same school walls were the birthplace of a movement that spread across New York. Now, a new generation of students painted alongside the legends who made that history. They paid tribute to the graffiti pioneers, the street art icons, and the teachers who kept the arts alive when budgets were cut. When you stand before "The Classics" at 730 East 12th Street, you are seeing a conversation between decades. The old school teaching the new school, and everyone picking up a brush.

column6: Christian Bachez, Toofly, Lorena Barrezueta Carlo, Kadeem Phillip
column13: Mural 700 was a milestone for Thrive Collective, and PS/MS 34 was the perfect place to celebrate it. "The Doer" by Christian Bachez, Toofly, Lorena Barrezueta Carlo, and Kadeem Phillip honors action over words. By 2025, Thrive Collective had painted 700 murals across New York City and beyond. That number represents thousands of students, hundreds of schools, and millions of brushstrokes. "The Doer" features a student with paint on their hands and determination in their eyes. They are not waiting for permission. They are making something happen. At 730 East 12th Street, in the same schoolyard where it all began, this mural asks every child a question. What will you do?

column6: Christian Bachez, Toofly, Lorena Barrezueta Carlo, Kadeem Phillip
column13: The Dreamer is the companion piece to "The Doer" at PS/MS 34, part of the Dream Walls 3.0 project in 2025. Artists Christian Bachez, Toofly, Lorena Barrezueta Carlo, and Kadeem Phillip created a mural that celebrates imagination as the first step toward change. The original Dream Walls project was named because it started with a dream. A few artists imagined grey concrete turning into color, and that dream became real. This mural shows a young person with their eyes closed, head tilted upward, surrounded by floating images of what they hope to become. When you look at "The Dreamer" at 730 East 12th Street, you are seeing the engine of every great achievement. You cannot do anything until you first dream it.

column6: Christian Bachez, Toofly, Lorena Barrezueta Carlo, Kadeem Phillip
column13: Some students are the first in their families to graduate high school. The mural "The Graduate" at PS/MS 34 honors that journey. Created in 2025 by Christian Bachez, Toofly, Lorena Barrezueta Carlo, and Kadeem Phillip as part of Dream Walls 3.0, the mural shows a cap and gown, a diploma, and a face full of pride. The Lower East Side has been a gateway for immigrant families for over a century. For many, a child's graduation is the culmination of years of sacrifice. The artists worked with students who were about to walk across their own stages. They painted what graduation meant to them. Some drew their parents crying happy tears. Others drew the jobs they would get. When you stand before "The Graduate," you are celebrating every late night of studying and every family that believed education was the way forward.

column6: Christian Bachez, Toofly, Lorena Barrezueta Carlo, Kadeem Phillip
column13: Every journey needs a path. The mural "The Path" at PS/MS 34, created in 2025 by Christian Bachez, Toofly, Lorena Barrezueta Carlo, and Kadeem Phillip, is a winding road of colors and choices. The Lower East Side can be a tough place to grow up, with pressures that pull kids in many directions. The artists asked students to paint the paths they wanted to take. Some drew college campuses. Some drew music studios. One student painted a path that led back to their own neighborhood because they wanted to become a teacher. "The Path" at 730 East 12th Street is not just a mural. It is a map of hopes. Every child walks past it and sees their own future reflected back.

column6: Christian Bachez, Toofly, Lorena Barrezueta Carlo, Kadeem Phillip
column13: Strong communities are built on strong pillars. The mural "The Pillars" at PS/MS 34, part of Dream Walls 3.0 in 2025, was created by Christian Bachez, Toofly, Lorena Barrezueta Carlo, and Kadeem Phillip to show what holds a school up. The artists asked students what pillars supported their lives. Answers included family, teachers, friends, faith, and art. Each pillar was painted as a colorful column, decorated with the faces and symbols that mattered most to the students. When you look at "The Pillars" at 730 East 12th Street, you are seeing the invisible made visible. Every hug from a grandmother, every after school program, every teacher who stayed late. That is what holds a community up.

In Prince George's County, Maryland, Tasker Middle School unveiled "We Serve" in 2025, created by artists Christian Penn and Ryan Mizta. Tasker Middle School has a focus on service and community responsibility. The artists worked with students to paint images of helping hands, food drives, and young people cleaning up local parks. The mural at 4601 Hill Road in Bowie is a reminder that middle schoolers are not too young to make a difference. When you stand before "We Serve," you are looking at the next generation of volunteers, activists, and neighbors. They are learning that leadership is not about being in charge. It is about showing up.

column1: Play in the Park: Mahoney Playground
column13: Staten Island's Mahoney Playground got a burst of color in 2025 thanks to artists Cody Prez, Cramcept, and John Exit. The "Play in the Park" series included a mural simply called "Dance." After years of pandemic isolation and economic stress, Staten Island families needed places to celebrate again. The artists painted figures mid twirl, arms outstretched, faces lit up with joy. The mural at 87 Crescent Avenue is an invitation. Dance in the park. Dance in the street. Dance because you are alive. When you look at it, you can almost hear the music.

column1: Play in the Park: Mahoney Playground
column13: Share was another mural in the Mahoney Playground "Play in the Park" series on Staten Island, created in 2025 by Cody Prez, Cramcept, and John Exit. In a world that often tells us to hold on tight to what we have, this mural shows hands passing food, books, and toys from one person to another. The artists worked with local children who drew their favorite things to share. A slice of pizza. A basketball. A crayon. The finished work at 87 Crescent Avenue is a lesson painted in bright colors. Sharing does not make you have less. It makes your community have more.

column1: Play in the Park: Mahoney Playground
column13: Dream joined the "Play in the Park" series at Mahoney Playground on Staten Island in 2025, created by Cody Prez, Cramcept, and John Exit. Every child who runs through this playground has a dream, but not every child has someone who asks what it is. The artists asked. They painted the answers on the wall. Spaceships, veterinarian offices, basketball courts, Broadway stages. The mural at 87 Crescent Avenue is a permission slip. It says you are allowed to dream big, even if no one else in your family has ever done what you want to do. When you look at it, you are looking at the future, one dream at a time.

column1: Play in the Park: Mahoney Playground
column13: Grow was painted at Mahoney Playground on Staten Island in 2025 by artists Cody Prez, Cramcept, and John Exit as part of the "Play in the Park" series. Children grow so fast, and sometimes adults forget to notice. This mural shows seeds becoming sprouts, sprouts becoming flowers, and flowers reaching toward the sun. The artists worked with local kids who drew themselves at different ages. A baby. A kindergartner. A high school graduate. When you stand before "Grow" at 87 Crescent Avenue, you are watching a time lapse of a childhood. It is a reminder to pay attention. The growing is happening right now.

column1: Play in the Park: Mahoney Playground
column13: Love was a natural addition to the "Play in the Park" series at Mahoney Playground on Staten Island in 2025, created by Cody Prez, Cramcept, and John Exit. Not money. Not rules. Love. The artists painted hearts of all sizes, families hugging, and friends walking arm in arm. The mural at 87 Crescent Avenue is soft and warm, a contrast to the hard concrete of the city. When you look at it, you are seeing the invisible thread that ties neighbors to neighbors. It is easy to forget to say it. This mural says it out loud. Love.

column1: Play in the Park: Mahoney Playground
column13: Believe was part of the "Play in the Park" series at Mahoney Playground on Staten Island in 2025, painted by Cody Prez, Cramcept, and John Exit. Not just religious faith, but faith in yourself, in your family, and in tomorrow. The artists asked children what they believed in. Answers ranged from God to good grades to their own two hands. The mural at 87 Crescent Avenue became a collection of those beliefs, painted in bold letters and bright images. When you stand before "Believe," you are seeing trust made visible. Every child who passes it is reminded that someone believes in them. That is a powerful thing.

column1: Play in the Park: Mahoney Playground
column13: Peace was painted at Mahoney Playground on Staten Island in 2025 by Cody Prez, Cramcept, and John Exit as part of the "Play in the Park" series. Not wealth or fame, but peace. The artists painted doves, olive branches, and children sitting together in calm quiet. The mural at 87 Crescent Avenue is an antidote to the noise of the city. It is a deep breath painted on a wall. When you look at it, you are seeing a wish. That arguments can end. That differences can be set aside. That a playground can be a place of peace.

column1: Play in the Park: Mahoney Playground
column13: Cheer joined the "Play in the Park" series at Mahoney Playground on Staten Island in 2025, created by Cody Prez, Cramcept, and John Exit. Life is hard, but there is always something to cheer about. The artists painted megaphones, pom poms, and smiling faces. They worked with local children who drew their biggest cheers. A soccer goal. A good grade. A birthday party. The mural at 87 Crescent Avenue is pure joy on a wall. When you look at it, you might find yourself smiling. That is the point. Cheer is contagious.

column1: Play in the Park: Mahoney Playground
column13: Jump was painted at Mahoney Playground on Staten Island in 2025 by Cody Prez, Cramcept, and John Exit as part of the "Play in the Park" series. Every great thing in life requires a leap. The artists painted children jumping rope, jumping into puddles, and jumping for joy. The mural at 87 Crescent Avenue is full of motion and energy. When you look at it, you are seeing a metaphor. You cannot cross a chasm in two small steps. You have to jump. This mural tells every child who sees it to take that leap.

column1: Play in the Park: Words To Inspire
column13: Words To Inspire was a series within the larger "Play in the Park" project at Mahoney Playground on Staten Island in 2025, created by Cody Prez, Cramcept, and John Exit. The first mural simply said "Play." Adults forget to play, but children should not. The artists painted the word in big, bouncy letters, surrounded by images of hopscotch, tag, and swing sets. The mural at 87 Crescent Avenue is a command and an invitation. Play. Not as a reward for finishing homework. Play as a right. When you look at it, you are being reminded that childhood is short. Play while you can.

column1: Play in the Park: Words To Inspire
column13: Thrive was another "Words To Inspire" mural at Mahoney Playground on Staten Island in 2025, painted by Cody Prez, Cramcept, and John Exit. To thrive means more than just surviving. It means growing, flourishing, becoming your fullest self. The artists painted the word "Thrive" in bold letters, surrounded by images of plants, children reading, and families laughing. The mural at 87 Crescent Avenue is a promise to every child who plays there. You are not just supposed to get by. You are supposed to thrive.

column1: Play in the Park: Words To Inspire
column13: Create was the final "Words To Inspire" mural at Mahoney Playground on Staten Island in 2025, created by Cody Prez, Cramcept, and John Exit. We are makers. From cave paintings to TikTok videos, humans have always created. The artists painted the word "Create" alongside images of paintbrushes, guitars, and dance shoes. The mural at 87 Crescent Avenue is a reminder that creativity is not a luxury. It is a part of who we are. When you look at it, you are being invited to make something. Anything. A drawing, a song, a story. Just create.

The Queens HeART Beat Festival in South Jamaica got a new mural in 2025 called "Stay Connected," created by artist Colleen Kong Savage. After the isolation of the pandemic, South Jamaica needed ways to bring people back together. Kong Savage painted images of cell phones, holding hands, and neighborhood windows with lights on. The mural at 177-01 Baisley Boulevard is a reminder that connection is not automatic. You have to choose it. When you stand before "Stay Connected," you are seeing a prescription for loneliness. Call someone. Wave at a neighbor. Stay connected.

column1: FDR High School: The Brooklyn Way
column13: FDR High School in Mapleton, Brooklyn, unveiled "The Brooklyn Way" in 2025, created by artists Cramcept and Yukiko Izumi. Brooklyn has its own culture, its own slang, its own way of doing things. The artists worked with students to paint what "The Brooklyn Way" meant to them. Some drew pizza slices and subway trains. Others painted brownstones and block parties. The mural at 5800 20th Avenue is a love letter to the borough. When you look at it, you are seeing students claim their identity. They are not just New Yorkers. They are Brooklynites. That is a different thing entirely.

column2: Soundview Academy for Culture and Scholarship
column13: Soundview Academy in the Bronx got a mural makeover in 2025, and the first mural was "Courage," created by artist Danielle Mastrion. Soundview has a reputation for being tough, but the students there show courage every day just by walking through the doors. Mastrion worked with them to paint images of lions, superheroes, and ordinary kids doing extraordinary things. The mural at 1160 Colgate Avenue is a daily pep talk. You have courage. You have always had courage. When you look at it, you are seeing strength that the world often overlooks.

column2: Soundview Academy for Culture and Scholarship
column13: A second "Courage" mural was also created at Soundview Academy in 2025 by Danielle Mastrion. This one focused on the word itself, painted in bold letters across the wall. Sometimes you need to hear something more than once. The students helped choose the colors and the style, making the word their own. The mural at 1160 Colgate Avenue is simple but powerful. Every time a student walks past it, they see the word "Courage." Eventually, they start to believe it. When you look at this mural, you are seeing how art can change a mind, one glance at a time.

column6: Danielle Mastrion, Amber Smalls, Chey Nelson
column13: PS 123K in Bushwick, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2025 with an attitude. "Can't Stop / Won't Stop" was created by Danielle Mastrion, Amber Smalls, and Chey Nelson. Bushwick has been through waves of change, from industrial decline to artist lofts to luxury buildings. But the families who have been there for generations keep going. The artists worked with students to paint images of running shoes, finish lines, and determined faces. The mural at 100 Irving Avenue is a declaration. No matter what gets in your way, you keep moving. When you look at it, you are seeing the spirit of Bushwick itself. Unstoppable.

column1: SVA Mural Makeover: Embrace the Future
column2: Soundview Academy for Culture and Scholarship
column6: Danielle Mastrion, Pelumi Ayeni, Marissa Molina
column13: Embrace the Future was another mural in the Soundview Academy makeover in the Bronx in 2025, created by Danielle Mastrion, Pelumi Ayeni, and Marissa Molina. The future can be scary, but it can also be beautiful. The artists asked students to paint what they wanted the future to look like. They drew green parks, flying cars, and families still eating dinner together. The mural at 1160 Colgate Avenue is not a prediction. It is a wish. When you look at it, you are seeing young people refusing to be cynical. They believe the future can be better. That belief is the first step toward making it true.

PS 45Q in South Ozone Park, Queens, unveiled "Unify at PS 45" in 2025, created by Danielle Mastrion and Yvette Hidalgo. South Ozone Park is one of the most diverse neighborhoods in the world, with families from Guyana, Bangladesh, Mexico, China, and everywhere in between. The artists worked with students to paint flags, faces, and hands reaching across differences. The mural at 126-28 150th Street is a visual handshake. It says we are different, and that is our strength. When you look at it, you are seeing the United Nations in a schoolyard. That is the real America.

column10: 2581 Adam Clayton Powell Jr Blvd, New York, NY 10039
column13: Frederick Douglass Academy in Harlem got a mural in 2025 called "Lion's Pride," created by street art legend DAZE along with Steven Artiles and Ralph Demaio. Frederick Douglass Academy is named for the great abolitionist, and its mascot is the lion. The artists worked with students to paint a majestic lion surrounded by symbols of scholarship and strength. The mural at 2581 Adam Clayton Powell Jr. Boulevard is a reminder of who the students are expected to become. Leaders. Fighters for justice. Lions. When you look at it, you are seeing Douglass's dream carried forward by a new generation.

column10: 2589 Adam Clayton Powell Jr Blvd, New York, NY 10039
column13: PS 200 in Harlem got a companion mural in 2025 called "Affirmations," created by DAZE, Steven Artiles, and Ralph Demaio with help from Yasmine Rodriguez. What you say to yourself matters. The artists worked with students to paint positive statements on the wall. "I am smart." "I am kind." "I am enough." The mural at 2589 Adam Clayton Powell Jr. Boulevard is a daily dose of love for students who might not hear those words anywhere else. When you look at it, you are seeing the power of repetition. Say it enough times, and you start to believe it.

PS 60, The Alice Austin School on Staten Island, got a mural in 2025 called "Abundance," created by artist Jenna Morello. Many families on Staten Island live paycheck to paycheck. The word "abundance" might feel out of reach. Morello worked with students to paint images of overflowing gardens, full refrigerators, and families with plenty to share. The mural at 55 Merrill Avenue is not pretending that poverty does not exist. It is planting a seed. Abundance is possible. When you look at it, you are seeing a community choosing to believe in more.

Snug Harbor on Staten Island hosted the Illumin Arts festival in 2025, and the mural "Choose Kindness Always" was created by artist Jodi Dareal with a collective of young artists. Every day, you choose how to treat people. The mural at 1000 Richmond Terrace is covered in flowers, hearts, and gentle hands. It is a reminder that kindness is not weakness. It is strength. When you look at it, you are seeing young artists declare that they will be kind, even when the world is not.

column1: SI Tech HS: The Early Bird
column13: SI Tech High School on Staten Island got a mural in 2025 called "The Early Bird," created by artist Jodi Dareal. Successful people wake up early. They get started while others are still sleeping. The artists worked with students to paint images of morning routines, cups of coffee, and sunrises. The mural at 485 Clawson Street is a celebration of discipline. When you look at it, you are seeing students who understand that achievement is not magic. It is showing up, day after day, before anyone else is watching.

column1: Boone Avenue Walls: Don't Forget 2 Smile
column13: Boone Avenue Walls in the Bronx's Hunts Point neighborhood got a new mural in 2025 called "Don't Forget 2 Smile," created by Jodi Dareal and Christian Penn. Hunts Point has faced more than its share of pain, but the people there still smile. The artists painted bright faces, sunshine, and the words "Don't Forget 2 Smile" in playful letters. The mural at 1761 Boone Avenue is a command wrapped in a gift. When you look at it, you are being reminded that no matter how heavy life gets, a smile is still yours to give.

column1: The Shoppe: Don't Forget to Smile
column10: 440 New Dorp Ln, Staten Island, NY 10306
column13: The Shoppe and Sneaker Room on Staten Island got a mural in 2025 also called "Don't Forget to Smile," created by Jodi Dareal and Christian Penn. A sneaker store might seem like an unusual place for a mural, but the artists turned it into a gallery. The mural at 440 New Dorp Lane features smiling faces, colorful sneakers, and positive energy. When you look at it, you are seeing art meet everyday life. You do not need a museum. A smile can be a masterpiece.

column6: Jodi Dareal, Marie Stephen, Ralph Demaio
column13: PS 44 on Staten Island got a mural in 2025 called "We Are Eagles," created by Jodi Dareal, Marie Stephen, and Ralph Demaio. Eagles fly higher than other birds. They see further. The artists worked with students to paint eagles in flight, wings spread wide, against a bright sky. The mural at 80 Maple Parkway is a metaphor for every child in that school. You are not meant to crawl. You are meant to fly. When you look at it, you are seeing a community set high expectations. And then paint them on a wall.

column6: Jodi Dareal, Mimi Storm, Kel5mh, Loreto Hart, @yi_design_jp
column13: PS 53 in the Bronx's Concourse Village got not one but three murals in 2025. The first was "Reading is Fundamental," created by Jodi Dareal, Mimi Storm, Kel5mh, Loreto Hart, and yi_design_jp. Reading is the foundation of everything else. The artists painted books, letters, and children lost in stories. The mural at 360 East 168th Street is a celebration of the library and the classroom. When you look at it, you are seeing the simple truth that a child who reads becomes an adult who thinks. That is fundamental.

column6: Jodi Dareal, Mimi Storm, Kel5mh, Loreto Hart, @yi_design_jp
column13: The second mural at PS 53 in Concourse Village was "Reading is Fundamental 2," created by the same team. One mural was not enough to say everything that needed to be said. This companion piece focused on the joy of reading, not just the skill. The artists painted children laughing at funny stories, gasping at mysteries, and crying at sad endings. The mural at 360 East 168th Street is about falling in love with books. When you look at it, you are seeing the difference between reading because you have to and reading because you want to. That difference changes lives.

column6: Jodi Dareal, Mimi Storm, Kel5mh, Loreto Hart, @yi_design_jp
column13: The third mural at PS 53 was "Together We Shine," created by Jodi Dareal, Mimi Storm, Kel5mh, Loreto Hart, and yi_design_jp. No one shines alone. The artists painted stars, but each star was part of a constellation. The students helped design images of group projects, team sports, and family dinners. The mural at 360 East 168th Street is a lesson in humility. Your light is brighter when you stand next to others. When you look at it, you are seeing children learn that success is not a solo act.

column6: Jodi Dareal, Pelumi Ayeni, Motoko Otsuki
column13: PS/IS 178K in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2025 called "She's My Hero," created by Jodi Dareal, Pelumi Ayeni, and Motoko Otsuki. The artists asked students to name their heroes. Mothers, grandmothers, aunts, and teachers topped the list. The mural at 2163 Dean Street features portraits of real women from the students' lives, alongside superhero capes and crowns. When you look at it, you are seeing young people recognize the everyday heroism of the women who raise them. That recognition is a gift.

column6: Joshua Gabriel, Amber Smalls, Motoko Otsuki, Ralph Demaio
column13: CS 145 in Bushwick, Brooklyn, got two murals in 2025 called "My Bushwick Life." The first was created by Joshua Gabriel, Amber Smalls, Motoko Otsuki, and Ralph Demaio. Bushwick has changed rapidly, but the students' lives are the constant. The artists asked them to paint their daily routines. Walking to the bodega. Playing in the park. Eating with family. The mural at 100 Tompkins Avenue is a documentary in paint. When you look at it, you are seeing the real Bushwick, not the real estate ads or the crime stats. Just life.

column6: Joshua Gabriel, Amber Smalls, Motoko Otsuki, Ralph Demaio
column13: The second "My Bushwick Life" mural at CS 145 was created by the same team. This one focused on the future. The artists asked students where they wanted "My Bushwick Life" to lead. College. Careers. Families of their own. The mural at 100 Tompkins Avenue is full of images of diplomas, stethoscopes, and graduation caps. When you look at it, you are seeing ambition. These students love Bushwick, but they are not trapped by it. They are using it as a launchpad.

column6: Joshua Gabriel, Kadeem Phillip, Ralph Demaio, Andrea Amanda, May Bukwoski
column13: PS/MS 83X in the Bronx's Morris Park neighborhood got a mural in 2025 called "Collaboration, Initiative & Perseverance," created by Joshua Gabriel, Kadeem Phillip, Ralph Demaio, Andrea Amanda, and May Bukwoski. Schools do not just teach math and reading. They teach how to be a person. The artists worked with students to paint three pillars. People working together. People starting things. People refusing to quit. The mural at 1500 Rhinelander Avenue is a curriculum for a good life. When you look at it, you are seeing what PS 83X values most. Not test scores. Character.

column1: Queens Preparatory Academy: In Unity There is Strength
column6: Kadeem Phillip, Chey Nelson, Lola Lovenotes, May Bukowski
column13: Queens Preparatory Academy in Rochdale, Queens, got a mural in 2025 called "In Unity There is Strength," created by Kadeem Phillip, Chey Nelson, Lola Lovenotes, and May Bukowski. The world tries to pull people apart by race, class, and background. This mural pushes back. The artists painted interlocking hands, linked arms, and faces of many colors standing together. The mural at 143-10 Springfield Boulevard is a political statement painted by teenagers. When you look at it, you are seeing the next generation reject the hatred of the old one. In unity, there is strength. They believe it.

column6: Kadeem Phillip, Wale Ayeni, Mutoko Otsuki, Ralph Demaio, Joshua Gabriel, Raissa Oliveira Da Silva
column13: MS 484K in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2025 called "It Takes a Village," created by Kadeem Phillip, Wale Ayeni, Mutoko Otsuki, Ralph Demaio, Joshua Gabriel, and Raissa Oliveira Da Silva. It takes a village to raise a child. The artists painted that village. Parents, teachers, coaches, neighbors, and friends all surrounding a group of children. The mural at 430 Howard Avenue is a web of care. When you look at it, you are seeing the invisible village that every child needs. This mural makes it visible.

Another Boone Avenue Walls mural in Hunts Point was called "Family," created in 2025 by KEL5MH and Yvette Hidalgo. The artists painted images of parents and children, but also of close friends and mentors who became like family. The mural at 1761 Boone Avenue is warm and intimate. When you look at it, you are seeing the definition of family expand. Family is who shows up. Family is who loves you. That is what these artists painted.

The Mary Mitchell Center in the Bronx's West Farms neighborhood got a mural in 2025 called "Peace Builds Community," created by artist Kenneth Tooley. Peace is not just the absence of conflict. It is the presence of something better. Tooley worked with community members to paint images of people building things together. Houses, gardens, relationships. The mural at 2107 Mapes Avenue is a how to guide. If you want community, start with peace. When you look at it, you are seeing a blueprint for a better neighborhood.

PS 86Q in Jamaica, Queens, got several murals in 2025. The first was "Learn It for Yourself," created by artist Kristy McCarthy with Dorothy, the Cowardly Lion, the Scarecrow, and the Tinman from The Wizard of Oz. The Wizard of Oz is a story about characters who discover they already have what they were seeking. The artists painted those characters alongside students reading books and solving problems on their own. The mural at 87-41 80th Street is a lesson. No one can learn for you. You have to learn it for yourself.

Another PS 86Q mural in 2025 was "The Power Within," also created by Kristy McCarthy. The artists asked students what superpower they wished they had. The answers were surprising. Not flight or invisibility, but confidence, kindness, and focus. McCarthy painted those inner powers as glowing lights inside each student's chest. The mural at 87-41 80th Street is a reminder that you do not need to be bitten by a radioactive spider. The power was always inside you. When you look at it, you are seeing children discover their own magic.

The Bronx Museum of Art hosted an AACC project in 2025 called "Spread Love," created by artist Lola Lovenotes. For decades, the Bronx was portrayed as a place of decay and danger. But the people of the Bronx know it as a place of love. Lovenotes painted hearts, hugs, and the words "Spread Love" in bright, hopeful colors. The mural at 1040 Grand Concourse is a correction to the record. When you look at it, you are seeing the real Bronx. The one that takes care of its own. The one that loves.

column6: Lola Lovenotes, Raissa Oliveira Da Silva
column13: Harlem Week 2025 included a mural called "Love Heals," created by Lola Lovenotes and Raissa Oliveira Da Silva. Harlem has endured generations of systemic neglect, but love has always been the medicine. The artists painted images of healing hands, embraced bodies, and hearts being repaired. The mural on West 135th Street is a prescription. When you look at it, you are seeing art as therapy. Love does not fix everything, but it is the only place to start.

column1: IS 117X: Promoting Change in our World
column6: Lola Lovenotes, Raissa Oliveira Da Silva
column13: IS 117X in Mount Hope, Bronx, got a mural in 2025 called "Promoting Change in our World," created by Lola Lovenotes and Raissa Oliveira Da Silva. Young people are often told they are too young to make a difference. This mural disagrees. The artists worked with students to paint images of protests, petitions, and peaceful rallies. The mural at 1865 Morris Avenue is a call to action. When you look at it, you are seeing teenagers who refuse to wait for adults to fix things. They will promote change themselves.

column6: Lola Lovenotes, Raissa Oliveira Da Silva, Ralph Demaio, Motoko Otsuki
column13: Another Harlem Week mural in 2025 was called "Art Heals," created by Lola Lovenotes, Raissa Oliveira Da Silva, Ralph Demaio, and Motoko Otsuki. When words fail, art speaks. The artists painted people making art in all its forms. Painting, dancing, singing, writing. The mural on West 135th Street is a celebration of creation as healing. When you look at it, you are seeing a community choose the paintbrush over the sword. Art heals. They believe it because they have lived it.

Kings Plaza Mall in Mill Basin, Brooklyn, got a mural in 2025 created by artist Marissa Molina. Malls are not usually places for murals, but Kings Plaza wanted to change that. Molina painted a colorful, abstract celebration of Brooklyn diversity. The mural at 5100 Kings Plaza is a surprise in a shopping center. When you look at it, you are seeing art sneak into unexpected places. That is how culture spreads. One mall, one wall, one moment at a time.

PS 13K in East New York, Brooklyn, got three murals in 2025. The first was "Checkmate," created by Marissa Molina. Chess is a game of thinking ahead, anticipating your opponent, and protecting your king. Molina painted chess pieces on a board, but the pieces were students and teachers. The mural at 557 Pennsylvania Avenue is a lesson in life. Every move matters. Think before you act. When you look at it, you are seeing East New York children learn to play the long game.

The second PS 13K mural was "Keys for Inspiration," also by Marissa Molina. Every child has a locked door inside them. The key is different for each one. Music, sports, art, or science. Molina painted giant keys labeled with different passions, surrounded by students holding them. The mural at 557 Pennsylvania Avenue is an invitation. Try every key. One of them will open your door. When you look at it, you are seeing the beginning of a lifelong search.

The third PS 13K mural was "Raising the Bar," also by Marissa Molina. Low expectations are a trap. High expectations are a ladder. Molina painted students lifting a bar higher and higher, with smiles on their faces. The mural at 557 Pennsylvania Avenue is a challenge. Do not settle. Do not let anyone tell you what you cannot do. Raise the bar. When you look at it, you are seeing children who refuse to be limited.

column4: Atlantic Avenue under the BQE, Brooklyn, NY 11201

column13: The Atlantic Avenue BQE murals in Brooklyn were a massive 2025 project under the Brooklyn Queens Expressway. Multiple artists created a series of murals. The first was "North Wall," a sweeping celebration of the neighborhood's history and people. Highways usually divide communities, but these murals tried to heal. The location at Atlantic Avenue and Columbia Street is under the shadow of the BQE. The artists turned that shadow into color. When you look at it, you are seeing a community reclaim its space.

column1: Atlantic Avenue BQE Murals: North Wall
column4: Atlantic Avenue under the BQE, Brooklyn, NY 11201
column6: Marissa Molina, Christian Penn, Will Power, Vince Ballentine, Jodi Dareal, Michela "Miki Mu" Muserra, Peach Tao
column10: Atlantic Ave & Columbia St, Brooklyn, NY 11201
column13: Restore was another Atlantic Avenue BQE mural in 2025. The BQE is crumbling. The neighborhood has been neglected. But restoration is possible. The artists painted images of rebuilding, fixing, and healing. Scaffolding became beautiful. Construction became art. The mural at Atlantic Avenue and Columbia Street is a promise. We will restore what was broken. When you look at it, you are seeing hope painted on concrete.

column1: Atlantic Avenue BQE Murals: North Wall
column4: Atlantic Avenue under the BQE, Brooklyn, NY 11201
column6: Marissa Molina, Christian Penn, Will Power, Vince Ballentine, Jodi Dareal, Michela "Miki Mu" Muserra, Peach Tao
column10: Atlantic Ave & Columbia St, Brooklyn, NY 11201
column13: Recreate joined the Atlantic Avenue BQE series in 2025. The same team of artists asked what it means to recreate. Not just to rest, but to make something new. They painted scenes of people turning old things into new things. A junkyard becoming a garden. A vacant lot becoming a playground. The mural at Atlantic Avenue and Columbia Street is an imagination engine. When you look at it, you are seeing permission to rebuild your world exactly as you want it.

column1: Atlantic Avenue BQE Murals: North Wall
column4: Atlantic Avenue under the BQE, Brooklyn, NY 11201

column10: Atlantic Ave & Columbia St, Brooklyn, NY 11201
column13: Biodiversity was another mural in the Atlantic Avenue BQE series in 2025. Under the highway, you might not expect to see plants and animals. But the artists painted butterflies, birds, and flowers thriving in unexpected places. The mural at Atlantic Avenue and Columbia Street is an ecological lesson. Life finds a way. Even under concrete, even in the shadows, nature persists. When you look at it, you are seeing resilience in every color.
